div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Garden Parties.—Sir Henry and Lady Bellingham are next week to entertain Lord and Lady Aberdeen at Bellingham Castle; the scene of a garden party this week, a congratulatory festivity,on the birth of a grand- son, the future 'Marquis of Bute. The Castle has a romantic history, and the grounds are ideally adapted for a garden party, although one never quite knows what to do at such entertainments. One can enjoy a picnic, or a visit to a country house when it is possible to do as one likes, play a game of tennis, or croquet, but at the conventional garden party, the games are soon monopolised and all one can do is to sit and talk banalities with all and sundry,whilst people one doesn't like glare at onecend criticise ones clothes. One says and hears the same remarks about the gardens, and arrangements over and over again, and generally make believe one is enjoying it immensely, while all the time planning a vanishing ruse, or evolving a decent excuse for going home. The men are more bored than the women, whilst the hostess—all smiles and graciousnass—is but longing for it all to be over. A few succeed in making a garden party enjoyable, but the formal and dressing affair that goes by that name is of a different order—a whited sepulchre of an entertainment.

Teachers and Golf.—Dr. Macnamara's recommenda- tion of golf as an ideal recreation for jaded teazhers presumably applies to women as well as to men, but unlike croquet or tennis, golf is an expensive pursuit, and is probably beyond the means of the great majority of teachers. Apart from this drawback golf has every- thing to recommend it, providing as it does both mental absorption and bealth-giving exercise. Whether it is Conducive to making one a model of self-control, so necessary in the cbararrer of a teacher, is not so certain.. There are features about golf that appear to vex the player in a far greater degree than is the case with other games. It is something like conjuring—you I may know perfectly well how the tricks should be done, I but, unless you have some of the art of the conjuror, you cannot do them. So it is at golf. No doubt many teachers find the tables turned on them when playing it, and are told of their faults by a small caddie, but, although you may know that you can keep, the right arm too stiff, or stand too much in front, or too far away, or take the eye off the ball, it still remains the exception rather than the rule to get in a clean hit ball,' and it is the many failures and mishaps, that evoke ' those explosions of temper for which golf is notorious. Victimizing the Holiday-Maker.—Artists and writers vie with one another in picturing the tribulations which, await the family in starting for A° holidays and spend- ing a fortnight in lodgings at the seaside. It is a 5 familiar subject in all the comic papers, and still does duty despite' the fact that there has been in recent years a distinct improvement in the class and character of the modern lodging-house landlady. It is true that it is always best to inquire if there are " extras "and to ask particularly what they are. "Cruet" is a very common item, and it is not advisable to follow the example of the lodger who took sway the cruet stand, and after- wards had to explain to the police magistrate that he thought he had boueht it. Still the average lodging- house landlady has risen above the petty pilferings, the "accidents," the depredations of the "cat.," that were characteristic of the old-fashioned type. On the other hand the long shoremen appear to have degenerated, if one is to accept views of a writer in one of the magazines. The dodge is to work a casting-net between, a Seine boat and the shore, and to get the sporting holiday-maker to offer 2s. Gd. or ss. for the catch, when at the best, this is not likely to be worth more than a few pence. A aoral for our Holiday Resorts.—The Rev. C. H. Gruady, who is a well-known writer on popular subjects, prefaced his own vacation by preaching on "The use and abuse of holidays." The subject sounds like a week-day one, but Mr. Grundy found in it a very suit- able theme for a sermon, impressing upon his people the duty of unselfishness, and thoughtfulness for others, as well as the importance of spending Sunday well.' One point Mr. Grundy especially emphasised, viz., that there is no country in the world with so many splendid holiday resorts as are to be found in the British Isles. That is a fact which numbers of people who go abroad for their holidays are prone to ignore and there is no need to wonder why foreigners who come to us in the summer should ask why we desire to spend our holidays abroad, when we have such beautiful scenery and surpassing loveliness stretched before us at home. Woman's Neglect of "her proper sphere."—Woman's desertion of the domestic hearth, is the constant theme of the theorists and the moralists, and the subject was even discussed at the re3ent British Association meet- ing. It was suggested that before marriage a woman should produce some evidence of domestic training. just the samf, as the man is supposed to show evidence of means to support a wife. But is it a fact that the domesticated girl is the most sought after? There are many who think that it is not so. Those who would set bock the feminine world to the crinoline period, forget that woman did not have the best of times in those days. There is nothing very exhilarating in domestic drudgery, and that was generally her lot, whilst men had most of the pleasures of life. Formerly ' spinsterhood was a thing to be half-ashamed of, and apologised for, hut if it is different now it is because women heve revolted against the unequal division of domestic burdens, and prefer to be self-supporting and independent. One is struck by the little regard that is shown for this point of view in the tirades of the theorists and moralists on woman's neglect of what they choose to call her proper sphere.

• A Universal Langaage.—One cannot but admire the perseverance of the Esperantists, who have been meet- ing in Congress at Cambridge. So far from being dis- mayed by the failure of many previous schemes for the establistment of a universal language, they appear con- fident that their efforts to extend a model human tongue will eventually succeed. One of the earliest attempts to formulate a dialect which " surmounteth all the languages of the world," was made by Sir Thomas Urquhart, of Cromarty, in 1653, but nothing came of it, or of the many schemes which at one time or another have been subsequently brought out. Those who are not enthusiastic on the subject will doubtless expect to see Esperanto disappear with the rest, but of course such is not the opinion of its votaries. Tartan's Again.--It seems desperately bard lines, with our pretty summer toilettes still barely worn, to think about warm woollen coats and skirts, yet the fact remains that early next month we shall need such garments, and that every day the tailors are getting busier, and less likely to give us, as they say their "best attention." As usual, at this season of the year,tartans are greatly to the fore, often of so weird a design as no sialf-respecting Scot would bring himself to recognise. Provided however we place such fabrics in the hands of really first class tailors, they should prove undeniably attractive, and look particularly well with a background of sea or shore, heather-covered moor, or mountain-side, but if we cannot afford such a luxury a tartan decidedly subdued in colouring, and very simple in design, is the wiser choice. Relief can so easily be afforded by means of a brightly hued collar, a touch of the same colour appearing on the cuffs.

Autumn Millinery.—Signs of autumn are apparent in the milliner's showrooms, where velvet, felt, and drawn taffetas shapes are taking the place of, straws. Huge wings form the trimming most in demand, while next in favour come the speckled feathers of the pheasant, and quills gathered from the farmyard. Later, birds will again be worn, which is a matter for very real regret. Apparently nothing can be said or done to induce a considerable number of women to give up this particularly heartless and altogether objectionable mode The bell-shape seems likely to retain its hold upon our effections during the autumn so say authorities in the matter, and will no doubt be in evidence throughout the winter.

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
FEMININE FOOTWEAR.

"Women can hardly give too much attention to their feet," advised a " beauty " specialist. "The carriage and walk may be seriously im- paired by ill-fitting shoes, or pedal troubles such as corns and bunions. This is especially the case with women whose occupations keep them much on their feet. Headaches, nervous affections, wrinkles, and haggard looks are oc- casionally due to these clauses. Women whose feet are unshapely should never advertise the fact by wearing shoes of conspicuous colour or appearance. The beautiful foot may be empha4 sised in these ways, but the plain one should conceal itself in unassuming footgear. High heels are bad, in either case, as_they involve a physical strain that is not compensated for by the extra height they give."
EMPIRE VOILE FROCK.

..reen-ant e striped voile is employec.. or the realisation of this charming gown. Made somewhat in the Empire style, the full pleated skirt falls gracefully from a high, draped belt of soft green taffetas, and the hem is turned up with a broad stitched band of the same mate- rial. The full crossover bodice opens over a vest of white lace, and the sleeves finish at the

elbow with a sma puff and frill of lace. The smart little sleeveless coatee that completes this gown is of the green taffetas, and is trimmed with passementerie and fastened with handsome embroidered buttons and cords. With the gown is depicted a dainty white tulle ruffle, spotted with black chenille spots, and finished with long loops of black ribbon velvet. The hat, of white Leghorn, has a full crown of spotted net, and is trimmed with ono long black feather.

div.head: LIFE AND TIMES OF VICTORIA.
div.p: THE LIFE AND TIMES OF VICTORIA.

The compiler of the famous old book on "Royal and Noble Authors," if he were still liv- ing, would have some most interesting names to add to his work; but they would be chiefly in the section devoted to the authors of noble lineage. Fey in these modijrn days Royal per- sonages are usually much too busy for prolonged literary composition, ajid even the speeches of Royalty must nowadays be short. But Peers and Peereses have, as a rule, more leisure, and the fruit of it is often seen in books which seem subtly to reflect the distinction of their writers. First among Peer-authors, says M.A.P., must be reckoned the King's brotheryin-law, the Duke of Argyll, the great Scottish noble, whose blue eyes and fair hair are so characteristic of his race. From his statesman father he inherited a marked literary gift, which has shown itself in both prose and poetry. His term of office as Governor-General of Canada inspired him to write, not only those delightful travel-books, "Canadian Pictures" and "Memories of Canada and Scotland," but also an important work on Imperial Federation, at a time when that great ideal was not so fashionable as it is now. In the domain of hisfary come his excellent life of Pal- merston and his study of the United States after tho Civil War, as also his striking work on the life and times of Queen Victoria, his Royal mother-in-law. The Mac Cailean Mhor, to give him his Celtic title, has also written some charm- ing poems, the libretto for an opera, and a me- trical version of the Psalms.

div.head: PRACTICAL HOLIDAY FROCK.
div.p: PRACTICAL HOLIDAY FROCK.

Linen or navy-blue serge would be the most suitable material for the simple holiday frock de- picted in the sketch. For a cool, every-day frock it could be carried out in butcher-blue linen. The skirt is arranged in deep-set pleats, turning from the centre front. The pinafore i bodice s attached to the skirt at the waist, the material being arranged in large stitched pleats or tucks about the shoulders. The sailor collar

is square across the back ,nts tapering down as far as the waistline. It is trimmed with a border of white broderie anglaise; or it might be embroidered in a simple design in white flax thread. The blouse worn beneath is of white muslin spotted with blue, and is trimmed with rows of white lace insertion and finished at the neck with a frill of narrow lace, the full sleeves being drawn into little turn-back cuffs edged with insertion and lace.
THE TITLE OF "LADY."

We all like to have nice things said of us and to us, and when we think of the time-honoured title of "lady" as meaning a well-bred woman, it does seem a pity to discontinue its use, as has been suggested by persons who, without thinking of the question, would abolish it alto- gether. We admit that the term is often mis- applied; but the same thing may often be said as regards "gentleman." We have seen the flush of pleasure overspread the features of a hard-working woman as she rose to leave a railway carriage when someone said: "This lady is getting out here," and the simple dig- nity with which the title was accepted proved the implied comnliment had given happiness. There is an indefinable charm about the word. " lady" which gives power, when addressed re- spectfully to the woman, of whatever station, to bring out her best self. and the woman who strives to do her best, though in a humble posi- tion, is as much entitled to be called a lady as her sister who owes all to the accident of birth or position. The word 4'gentleivoman" has quite another meaning. For a woman to be such she must be of good birth and breeding. It is a sweet, old-fashioned word, and many an Englishwoman of gentle birth would prefer it to the word lady.

div.head: VERDICT OF THE HEART.
div.p: THE VERDICT OF THE HEART.
By CHARLES GARVICE,
Author of "Her Heart's Desire," "In Cupid's Chains," "Just a Girl," t'Nance," "The Out- cast of the Family," "A Coronet of Shame," dm

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: The •story opens in Australia, where Ralph Farringdon is-present at the deathbed of his mother. They .-soor, and she has been deserted by her husband, _.alph's step-father. With almost her last breath, she tells Ralph of papers in her box which are of importance to him. Her words are overheard by a man with the appearance of a tramp, who steals into the house and abstracts the contents () the box. The scene then changes to. Lynne Court, where Lord Lvnborough, aged and in fail- ing health, is in residence, his beautiful 'niece, Veronica Denby, ruling the household as chate-, One day the‘Eall sends for Veronica and informs her that it isins intention to leave her by will 'his whole fortune, his nephew, Talbot Deohy, succeeding only to the title and the entailed estates. He asks if she will accept the condition that she wed only a'man of title. Veronica, who is as proud as she is fair, and i*ho has known grinding poverty during her father's life, readily consents. Riding afterwards' on the neighbauring moor she is struck with the gallant act of a young stranger, who snatches a puppy from under her horse's feet, receiving some slight injury in con- sequence. He refuses pecuniary reward, but asks to be taken on as one of the Earl's _gamekeepers. -Lord Lvnborough,' coming up in his carriage, refers the applicant to his head man. The stranger, who gives the name of Ralph Farringdon, and says he has come from Australia obtains the., coveted job. The reader is now taken to London, and Talbot Denby is introduced—a.rising . young Con- servative M.P., ambitious, talented, but a con- firmed gambler of ,the worst type. Veronica sees Ralph Farringdon fishing in the park stream, and ;a at once attracted and irritated by the ease of manner towards her, which is not that of a dependant. He shews her how to throw the line, and in her attempts she gets the hook in her wrist. Ralph cuts it out, and, applies his lips, to the wound to draw out any possible poison. At that moment, Talbot Denby—who has been informed of the Earl's testamentary resolve, and hence 'wishes to marry Veronica—comes upon the pair. Talbot insults Ralph, who replies coolly, and meets a threat of violence by seizing Denby's stick and breaking it. Talbot complains to the Earl, who, however, after hearing Ralph's version of the affair, takes no action.

div.head: CHAPTER IX.
div.p: CHAPTER IX.

Ralph had not forgotten the trout he had been "ordered" to leave at the Masons', and, having cleaned it, he took it up to the cottage as he started on his evening round. He had intended leaving it with "Miss Veronica's compliments," but Fanny came running down the little garden path to meet him, and, with a blush and smile of welcome on her pretty face, pressed him to enter.

"Oh, you must come in and let mother thank you, Mr. Ralph!" she said, apparently out of breath with her short run. "She'll be so dis- appointed. Besides, you can't be in such a terrible hurry." "Terrible" was the favourite Lynne adjective, and it came very expessively from Fanny's pretty lips. -I.alph went in; she drew a chair up for him, und took his cap and put it on the sideboard, placed the fish on a dish, and called her mother in to admire the gift. "01, but you must thank Miss Denby," said Ralph. "The fish belongs to her—at least, Lord Lynborough—and she ordered me to leave it." Fanny smiled incredulously. "All very fine, Mr. Ralph, but we can guess who put it into her head. Oh, we know you gentlemen don't like being thanked, don't we, mother? And now you're here you must have some supper. See, I was just laying the cloth. He must, mustn't he, mother, or we shall think he didn't want us to have the trout; and you're so fond of it, aren't you, mother? And it's so nice to see anyone, and to have a talk. I'm sure life's dreary enough, with nothing but work, work, work all day!" "Well, but I musn't stay long," said Ralph, yielding to the soft voice and pleading persist- ence. He MO still sore from Veronica's treat- ment of him and Fanny's evident desire for his company soothed the wound to self-love which the proud Miss Denby had so wantonly inflicted. Fanny bustled about, but not noisily or obtrusively, and laid the supper, and Ralph was bidden with a winning smile to draw his chair up to the table. It was a change from the almost silent meals with the grim and taciturn I3urchett, and Ralph enjoyed not only the good, '.hough simple fare, but Fanny's bright smiles .nu girlish laughter. Her fair face was flushed with pleasure; she was as gay as a young linnet, and as soft as a dove, and she almost cooed as she pressed him to take some more butter. "I saw you fishing this morning," she said, as Mrs. Mason began to clear the things away; "you and Miss Veronica. Oh, do light your pipe! I know you men like to smoke the moment after you've eaten anything. I suppose you were teaching her? How clever she is, isn't she? And don't you think she's very beautiful? I do ! "

"Yes, oh, yes; I suppose she is," admitted Ralph, but without a corresponding enthusiasm. He was not altogether guileless, and he knew timt the best of women find it difficult to listen with pleasure to the praise of another's looks. "Oh, you only suppose? She is—you know she is. I'm sure everybody must admire her. And she's so sweet and kind hearted."
"Oh, is she ? " said Ralph, rather drily. "I can't say I've noticed that; but you know her better than I do—or ever shall do, I daresay I"

"I'm going up to the Court to-morrow,". said Fanny, archly, and I've a great mind to tell her what you say." "With all my heart!" laughed Ralph, but with a sudden heigntening of colour. "It strikes me that she wouldn't feel very interested in my opinion of her." "Oh, I don't know," said Fanny, with an ..ziectation of candour. "It isn't everybody Miss Veronica takes notice of, and if I were in your place I should feel highly flattered at I having her fishing with me. In fact, I consider you a very lucky man' Mr. Ralph." "Thank you, Miss Fanny," said Ralph rather ruefully, and inwardly wincing; "though I don't quite see where the luck comes in," he added, as he recalled his snubbing of the morning. "And now I must go on my rounds." . "Oh, you needn't hurry," she remonstrated. "You're early yet." "How do you know ? " retorted Ralph with a • laugh, and some surprise. Fanny coloured. She could not confess that she watched him every evening, and that most of . his comings and goings were known to her. I "Oh, I only guessed it because I wanted you to stay," she said, shyly. "Just five minutes . more, while you finish•your pipe!" Be was indeed earlier than usual, and, of course, Ralph yielded; and as he leant back in the comfortable Albert chair, as the big kitchen ones with arms are called, Fanny got out her work and sat on the other side of the table, • every now and then glancing 'out of the corner of her soft brown eyes at the handsome but somewhat pensive face. I "So Mr. Talbot's gone back to London," she said presently. "What a handsome gentleman lie is, isn't he ? " Ralph nodded absently. "Yes; he's a good- • lookinc,6 chap," he assented. "Such a distinguished - looking gentleman," murmured Fanny, still watching him out of the corner of her eyes. " Yes ; oh, ps," assented Ralph again. "I wonder if there's any truth in what they say—that he and Miss Veronica are going to inske a match of it ? " _

Ralph looked up quickly, then as suddenly became engrossed in stopping the tobacco in his pipe. "Oh, do they say so ? " he said, indifferently. "Yes," replied Fanny, with a knowing nod of her yellow head. "You son, it would be a good match for both of them. Miss Veronica would be a Countess, and Mr. Talbot would get his lordship's money. Oh, perhaps I oughtn't, to have said that, for it's a kind of secret that the Earl's going to leave Miss Veronica his money. I heard it from his lordship's gentleman, Mr. Welford, you know. But there! there's •rio harm in telling you, Mr. Ralph." "Not the least in the world," Ralph assured her: "especially as it is no business of mine and I've a habit of forgetting anything Mat doesn't concern or interest me.' _ . _ - -
"I hope that doesn't apply to your friends ?" the murmured, shyly, with a sudden flush.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 17, 1907
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 17, 1907

"Why, of course not," responded Ralph, laughing. "One's friends are always interestii,g, Miss Fanny, and one's gratitude for their kindness keeps them in remembrance." "Then I mustn't forget you, Mr. Ralph," she said with a laugh, but with a tender emphasis on the "you." "The kindness is on your side," he said. "You're the first friends I've made in Lynne, you know." Her face, all aglow with pleasure, was turned to him. "Oh, how nicely you said that," she breathed. "And I know you won't forget us, or —or leave us for, any new ones." "Well, I've got to leave you now,' said Ralph, lightly. "I have to ket_ a sharp look-out in the western woods, for I suspect it has had some undesirable visitors lately." She rose-and went with him to the door and down the garden path. "How sweet the stocks smelt,'• said Ralph.

"Don't they! They always smell sweeter at night," she said. "Wait a minute." She ran across to a border, picked a fine blossom, and came back to him. "There is one for you." She raised the flower to her lips—there is only a little distance between the nose and the lips, Tou see—and held it up to him. "Let me put it in your coat for you—may I? " she asked, in a low voice.

"Thank you," said Ralph, with too calm a gratitude, for she sighed faintly as her hand went up to the lappel of his coat. She was very close to him, so close that he could feel her warm, sweet breath upon his cheek; and as she put the flower in its place and raised her face, with a murmured "There ! " its dainty fairness was so near to his lips that it would almost have been pardonable if they had traversed the few inches and met her half-parted ones upturned so invitingly to him. But Ralph was not a susceptible man, and— rara avis !—not one given to flirting, and it did not occur to him to kiss her.

"Thanks very much!" he said, with exasperat- ing cheerfulness. 'Jove! how sweet it smells! Good-night, Miss Fanny." She stood and watched him, all her heart in her eyes, as he strode away with his pipe in his mouth and his gun on his shoulder; then, biting the lips which he had so coldly ignored, she sighed heavily and went indoors. It was nearly dawn before Ralph returned to the hut and to bed, but tired as he was, he was not too tired to dream. And he dreamt that he was standing by the stream, that Mr. Talbot was thrashing him with a stick and that Miss Veronica was looking on and laughing. It was not a pleasant dream by any means, and Ralph awoke with a cry of rage and humiliation and in a wringing perspiration. That night at dinner Veronica wore a heavy gold bracelet, which covered the spot on het wrist, and she kept the old-fashioned ornament. on until her maid had left her for the night. Then she took it off slowly, and looked long and musingly at the little red spot her slender white wrist.

"Blood-poisoning is very bad, I imagine," slit thought, dreamily. "It is fatal sometimes; very often, I think. I suppose he knew that or he wouldn't have presumed, wouldn't have dared to—to do what he did." Her face flushed with sudden shame. "It is very humiliating. A gamekeeper! He is the first man who has kissed no no !—whose lips have touched me ! " Her eyes glowed angrily; then suddenly anger died out. "I Wonder whether there was any danger for him? If there was poison in the wound—to call so small a pin-prick a wound; it is too, ridiculous !—but if: there was, and he happened to have a scratch on his lips—game- keepers often get scratched by the briars and— and—and things. Oh, how idiotic I am! What has come to me? How angry he looked when I as good as ordered him out of the hall. His eyes blazed; he was going to say something. I was afraid; yes, I was actually trembling inside. Did he see it? No, no; I am too clever, too artful. I wonder what he thinks of me? Not difficult to guess. What could he think but that I am so foolishly proud and heartless a woman as to be incapable of gratitude incapable of feeling anything but offended with a man ,for attempting to save my life. I suppose he did save me, or did he take advantage of—of the accident? Ah, no, that's unjust! I'm old enough to know an honest man when I see him, and this man is honest and genuine, I'll stake my life—the life he saved! Oh, what nonsense! There was no danger; but there might have been. Oh, Veronica, my dear Veronfca, are you out of your senses that you cannot forget the whole thing, that you must dwell upon your adventure—hateful word !—with a young game- keeper as if it were of any consequence? Young; that's it. He is young, and ridiculously good- looking; that the reason." Her face flushed with the shame that ran though her like a fire. "I wish Lord Lynborough had let him go. But even he, so rarely moved one way or the other, seemed impressed by the man—seemed to feel his influence. A gamekeeper with influence!" , She laughed impatiently. 'lt is too absurd! lam growing morbid and—and sentimental. This life of slothful ease and luxury is sapping my usually strong and healthy mind. I'll take Sally for a thirty mile spin to-morrow." Sally was brought round soon after Eireakfast the next morning, and set off on the thirty mile run which was to dispel the "morbid" vapours which possessed her mistress. The mare was young and fresh, and, in the exuberance of her spirits, rose two or three times at starting; but Veronica's seat was well-nigh a perfect one, and she only laughed at Sally's preliminary antics, which subsided after her mistress had let her have head across the park. When the mare had quite settled down for the time being, Veronica turned her into the wood. She had not gone very far through it before Sally pricked up her ears and started, and a moment afterwards Ralph came from amongst the trees to the edge of the narrow path. He raised his cap, but Veronica, though— indeed, because her heart gave a sudden bound at sight of him—kept her eyes fixed on Sally's ears and ignored Ralph's salutation. But the moment she had passed him, she felt annoyed with herself.

"Now, why couldn't I have just bowed ? " she thought, irritably. "The man will think I am attaching importance to his—presumption!" Ralph shrugged his shoulders as he looked after her, then went his way. Fate chose to amuse herself with them that day as it had done on the previous one; for as, an hour later, he crossed the top of a spinney, he heard the thud of hoofs behind him, and looking round he saw the mare tearing along the meadow at breakneck pace. If she had not actually bolted she had very nearly done so, and Ralph, as he glanced at the wood towards which the mare was making, could not help thinking of the peril that awaited her rider from over-hanging boughs and treacherous undergrowth. He stood, leaning on his gun, and waited. Veronica had got all her weight on the bit, and succeeded in pulling up the mare on the edge of the wood and so close to Ralph that he saw she was riding on a snaffle. The significant fact dispelled his reluctance to address her; indeed, he would have done so if she had been his mortal foe. He went up to her and said, respectfully but with the unembarrassed frankness which Veronica had found so trying: "Forgive me, Miss Denby, but is it wise to ride your horse on a snaffle? She's young and fresh, I see." Veronica was hot with the struggle, and not in the sweetest of tempers. "I always ride her on the snaffle," she said, curtly. "It is easier than a curb, and really more effective. If you knew anything about horses--" A smile which displayed itself for an instant in his eyes nettled her. "But I suppose, like most men, you think you do."

"I was a cowboy once,'7 he said, simply. "And you've only one rein, Ib , see," ho added, going up to the mare and patting her. Sally, who had been fidgeting, sniffed at the hand which he slid over her nose—an old cowboy trick, one Ralph had practised on Burehett's dog—and then, apparently satisfied, stood still and nibbled coquettishly at his sleeve. "Now, that's rather risky, and if I were your groom I wouldn't allow it.
"You wouldn't allow!" repeated Veronica, with a tine smile.

"No. I suppose he's responsible," said Ralph. "Tiro reins to a snaffle; but you'd better have a curb—you needn't use it—for a younc, and hot- headed mare like this. She's a beauty, oh, yes! I admired her the other day; but she's a mare and they're not always reliable. If she had bolted— she looked precious near it !—and had carried you Into the wows—well, it would have been awk- ward."
"But I can pull her up; I 'did," said Veronica. "This time, yes," he said, coolly, "but you might not always be able to do so; and your life is too ovecious-" •

The blood rose to Veronica's face. "Will you please let go of my rein," she said, coldly. "I beg your pardon," said Ralph, the colony coming into his tanned face, his eyes flashing with something like anger.. "I meant any life was too precious to take such chances.' His hand fell from the rein, and, raising his cap, he turned and struck into the wood. He reached the hut, and was removing the • cartridges from his gun—a precaution he always took—when he heard something rushing and tearing through the brake, and was just in time to spring upon the mare which was thundering affrightly through the clearing, and catch her by the—of course broken—rein. "Just what I thOught ! " he said to himself. He tied the mare \up to a tree, then, with a sinking heart, he followed her tracks, and presently came upon Veronica,. She was seated on a mossy bank, with her head in her hand. She had lost her hat, and her glorious hair had come part:7 undone, one dark, glossy strand falling over her cheek. She started at the sound of his footsteps and tried to rise, but sank down again and looked up at him with a mixture of helplessness, displeasure, and defiance. "I have had an accident," she said, haughtily, but her voice shook, and Ralph's heart melted at her distress. "So I see. Are you hurt ? " he asked, trying to speak casually, but his anxiety displayed itself in his voice and in his eyes eloquently enough. "N —o, I don't think so," she replied. "My mare was startled by a hare that run under her nose, and bolted. The rein broke—and I was thrown." She endeavoured to laugh with self- contempt. "I don't think I am hurt—but I struck my head, and I feel—dizzy—" He nodded. "I know." ! "My mare—if she gets to the Court—Lord Lynborough may hear of it and be alarmed." "That's all right. I've got the mare," he said. "if I only had some water! Do you think you could come as far as the hut? Lean on my arm."

She rose, supported by his arm, and staggered a little. , "Lean on me," he said, almost with an air of command. "That's right. It's not far, but you know. You. only want some water and a rest. Ah, you're_ not going to faint ! " for her eyes • closed. I "No, no," she said in a low voice, and evidently struggling womanfully with her weak- ness. "I think I must have hurt my foot, it's so painful." "A sprain ! " he said, more to himself than to her. "You must not walk on it. Put your hand on my shoulder." "What—what are you going to do ? she asked. "Carry you," he said, simply. "I forbid you!" she said,tlie colour rushing to her face. "Not much use," he .retorted, as quietly as before. "To walk on a sprain is a silly thing. It will mean bed, or a sofa, for you, for months perhaps. Keep still, please." Her pride would not permit her to struggle with him, and she suffered him, under protest, to raise her in his arms. As he strode off with her slowly but firmly, the pain nearly made her faint again and her eyes closed; her head dropped lower and lower until, against her will, though, she strove with all her force to exert it, it rested ' on his shoulder. He carried her into the hut and put her on a chair. His heart was beating fast, but not with the exertion of carrying her, though Veronica was no feather; every vein in his body was tingling, he saw the lovely white face as through a mist. Theli he shook off the influence of her beauty. He went presently, and getting some water, put the cup to her lips. She drank some, breathing slowly and pain- fully, and wiping her lips with her handkerchief. He took it from her, and dipping it in the water, • bathed her brow, and in doing so unconsciously drew her head till it rested against him. The ifaintness passed, and she opened her eyes and \looked up at him with a vague, uncertain • dreaminess. , "Where ?—Ah, yes,'l remember she breathed. Then the 'colour rushed over the ivory of her face. "Thank you," she said, coldly, but her eyes were shy, as they still met his as if she could not withdraw them. "I —I am sorry you should have so Much trouble." Ralph tried to say the conventional "No trouble," but his voice died away in a mutter. She moved and winced. "Your foot," he said. "Let me see." "No, no!" she said, earnestly; "It is nothing —I can walk." She put her foot tp the ground, and he saw her lips writhe. "Oh, how shall I get to the Court!" "I'll go for a carriage," he said. must get that boot off first, or else— "No, no," she said again, but, disregarding her refusal, he knelt down and untied the boot. IThe foot was already swollen, and as he endeavoured to take off the boot, she winced again. Ho took out his knife and cut up the back of the boot and slid it off gently and skil- ' fully, and the small, shapely foot, already beginning to swell, rested in the palm Of his hand. I She leant back, but her eyes rested on his bent. head with a strange expression from which pride was quite absent. I "I seem born to give you trouble, "she said, in a low voice. i Ralph started. He was like a man in a dream. • Her helplessness, her sudden weakness, had j wiped away the resentment which her past treat- • ment of him had caused. His heart was aching with pity, and with something else that was at once a delight and a pain. I "No, no," he said, rather huskily. "It is fortunate I was near. I'll go for a carriage. But you must rest the foot. Let me bring another chair—no, there's a couch there. , Stop ! " as she tried to rise. He put his arms Iround her, and lifting her, though she struggled slightly and drew back, carried her to the couch. "You'll lie still; you won't attempt to get up while I'm gone ? " ho said, authoritatively. "No," she said, in a low voice, and with downcast eyes. "You will not be long ? " j 1r "I'll run—oh, I'll ride; I forgot the mare," he said. As he went to the door he met Burchett. "Oh, Burchett, Miss Denby's had an accident. I'm going for a carriage," he said, quickly. . Durchett frowned and glanced at Veronica. It was evident that he did not relish a tete-a-tete with the lady of the Court. "Stay here," he said. "I'll go. I know. I saw it." Ralph went back to the couch. Veronica opened her oyes and looked at him. , "You are back already ? " she said, faintly. I "Burchett's gone," he said, awkwardly. "I'll go outside. If—if you want me--" "Stay, please," she said. "I do—l do not wish to be left alone."
"But we
The horse?

CHAPTER X. Ralph stood beside the couch, looking at nothing in particular, and, for the:first time in his life, at a loss for words. Veronica lay with her eyes closed, but her mind was busy behind them. She was marvelling at the fate which threw her and this man together, which persisted in placing her under an obligation to him, and the wonder of the fact was too great to allow of resentment. Besides,the woman in her clamoured for admiration and gratitude. Her sex adore readiness and strength in the man. Ralph had been as prompt as he had been to save the puppy, and he had picked her up and carried her as if she had been a bundle of straws, and—almost as marvellous--he had done so with a self-posses- sion, or rather a forgetfulness of self, that had robbed his service of offence. No gentleman could have been more gentle, or more completely lost himself in his anxiety on her account. "I'm afraid your foot is painful ? " he said, at last finding his voice. She opened her eyes upon him. "Yes, it is. Do you think it will get better quickly? I should hate being lame, laid up, for any time." "You will have to rest it," he said. "I think it all depends upon keeping'quiet fora day or ,two. I once sprained my ankle when I was gold- digging, and, because I kept bopping about on it, I had it bad for a long time." - -

1 "Gold digging? You seem to have been a great ninny things," remarked Veronica. Ralph nodded. "Oh, yes, I've tried all sorts of things. Jack-of-all-trades and master of none, aa they say." "And yet you found time to go to school," mused Veronica, absently. "Yes." he said, and as he answered he reached for a chair and sat down a little behind her, so that he could see her face.

It m as still pale and a little weary, but Ralph I was struck by its loveliness, as he had not been I struck hitherto. Perhaps it was because it did not at that moment wear its usual expression _ of pride and hauteur; perhaps it was because' Fanny had dinned Miss Veronica's beauty into hi

ears. How graceful she was, stretched out al full length, one white hand en her bosom, the other hanging by her side like a plucked lily! Watching her sent a thrill, a semi of thrills, through him, such as he remembered feeling when he had looked at a beautiful picture in a London picture gallery into which he had strayed one day. He was conscious of a peculiar sensation of unrest, of disquieting N. .itfulness which was quite novel to him, and yet not altogether painful. "Yes, my mother was very anxious about ley schooling, and kept me to it. She Was rather out of the ordinary. I think she had—' ideas about her station,'. as you would say. I remember she was fond of telling me it was easy to be 'a gentleman.' I don't know what she meant, unless it was that any man could be a , gentleman if he chose. She was ambitious on My account."

"Why did you say as you would say '?" 1 Veronica, as if she resented the person.:: application of the phrase. Ralph laughed shortly., "I was only thinking of you as one of the gentry,' " he explained. Veronica coloured. "It was because you think I am very proud and—and contemptuous towards my—inferiors?" she asked in a low voice.

'"Well, yes," he said, coolly. "Oh, it's all right. You've something to be proud of. It's a fine thing to be nobly born, •I think—to be 'rich and powerful. I suppoSe I should be as proud as you—as the rest—if I were, gay, the nephew of an Earl."
Veronica tucked her hand under her cheek and turned to look at him.

"Will you move your chair so that I can see you, please," she said. He dragged the chair forward, and gazQd at the opposite wall as if he were having his photo- graph taken. "Thanks. It hurt my neck craning. So you think I am proud and contemptuous," she said, thoughtfully. "Do you know "—suddenly--" that I have not always been rich and powerful, as you call it. Do you know that I was once, and not'so very long ago, quite, quite poor ? " "No," he said, turning to her With his interest shining in his eyes. "Yes, I was," Veronica went on, vaguely thinking as she ooked, at him, that his eyes and lashes were almost too good looking for a man, and too expressive for a woman. "My father was very poor, so poor that there was not always enough food." As the pity and sympathy softened the surprise in his eyes, her voice grew lower and her own eyes grew misty. "We lived in a poverty-stricken neighbourhood, and found it hard to live even there.' I have done needle- work "—she held up her white hand with its taper fingers. "It was months after I had come to the Court before the marks of the needle wore off.'

Ralph's eyes moved to the white fingers and clung .o them. "I have worn shabby clothes have gone about with wet feet because my boots were in holes, and I had to tramp to the factory with my work, because I‹.ouldn't afford the penny for the 'bus." "Good Heavens! "he murmured with a sense of guilt; for her words sounded like an accusation against the world of which he was a member. 'But I consoled myself all the time with the thought of what I was—a Denby. Nothing could rob me of that consolation, and it supported me in the bitterest hour. That was pride, you'll say. I daresay it is because I have suffered so much that lam proud. Do you think if Charles I. had been snatched from the scaffold at the last moment and restored to power that he would not have been all the more proud because of the sufferings, the slights, the insults he had borne ? '

Ralph nodded. "I see," he said in a low voice. "But, after all, you had your consolation, your support. You knew you were of high birth, that one day you might climb on to your throne— as you have. Some of us have no such help in our troubles..and struggles. We're of the mud, and mud we must remain. We're hewers of wood and drawers of water--" He stopped and shook himself. "That's rot though, isn't it ? " he said, with a laugh. "Why, I've read some- where that half the House of Lords consists of men whose fathers, or they themselves even, have risen from the lower classes."

"Yes," she said. "In no country in the world has a man so many chances of rising to the highest position as in England." His eyes kindled and his face flushed; then he laughed and sighed in a breath. "Yes, I know ill that. I used to think that I'd fight my way and come out on top or some- where near it, but—oh, well, I'm a lazy sort of beast, and too easily satisfied. Give me a chop and a pipe, and the country to eat and smoke them in, and I'm content. As I said, my mother used to lecture me upon my future and try—poor dear soul !—to inspire me with ambition. And if she had lived, perhaps— But she died, and I'm just a gamekeeper." The statement of his status seemed to remind him' of the fact that he was talking too freely to the great lady. "Burchett's a long time," he said. "I suppose, he has had some difficulty in getting a carriage." "It could not be here yet," said Veronica. "Will you please put something under my foot? The couch is so hard."

He took one of his coats from a nail, and folding it, raised the injured foot as gently as a woman could have done, and placed it on the improvised pillow. "Thank you," said Veronica. "Are you suffering much pain ? " he asked, standing and looking down at her wistfully. "No; not now. I'm suffering most from hunger," she replied, with a smile. He looked round eagerly but helplessly. "There's nothing but bread and cheese," he said.

"Yes, give me some, please," she said. He sprang to the cupboard and brought some to her. "I'd make you a cup of tea, but there wouldn't be time. What a confounded time the carriage is!" "Oh, tea with cheese! They wouldn't go well together, would they ? " she remarked with a little grimace, as she took the plate. He saw that she found it awkward to hold it, and took it from her.

"I'll hold it," ho said. "I wish there was something better." "Oh, don't apologise," she said. "I've known the time when bread and cheese would have seemed a feast of luxury." "Why did you tell me that—that you were once poor ? " he asked, impulsively. She raised her eyes—they were very near his as he bent forward with the plate in his hand— and smiled pensively. "I—don't quite know. Perhaps I did not like you—anyone—to think that I was proud, proud of my birth and wealth. Perhaps it was because —oh, I don't know! How nice this is; though it's rather difficul• eating in this position." She made as if to raise herself higher on the hard horsehair cushion, and Ralph set down the plate quickly, and putting his arm round her, helped her into the desired attitude. , "Thanks," she said, softly. "You are very strong. I want to tell ,you that I am sorry I was rude to you yesterday.' Her eyes were raised to his for a moment, then were downcast again. The transition was so sudden, the glance of the violet eyes so heart-thrilling, that Ralph caught his breath. "You—rude—!" he stammered.

"Yes," she said, almost meekly, as she nibbled daintily at the bread and cheese, and looked at him with half-lowered lids. "I don't know what possessed me. I suppose it was temper. All women are bad tempered, you know." "No, no," he remonstrated-with an almost indignant denial. "Not all. You-----" "I am very " she said, demurely. "I always was. Pride and ill-temper go together, you know. How thirsty bread and cheese make one."

He sprang to the cupboard. "There's some beer," he said, doubtfully. "Water, please," she returned, smoothly. "Oh, thank you. But it was tmgrateful ts well as ill-tempered after all your kindness." Ralph's face went the colour of brickdust. "I —l—beg your pardon," he stammered. "I didn't think for the moment. I only thought— blood-poisoning, you know, it's very dangerous. But—great liberty--" -"Yes," she said, with a smile gleaming in her eyes, whose rays seemed to warm Ralph's heart. "It reminds me of the courtier who nearly let the King of Spain burn to death because it was nrt etiouette to tell him that his coat had cauclit alight at the lire before which his Majesty was standing." Ralph laughed, but it was a shaky laugh. "And you ran some risk," shesaid, in a low

voice. "Oh, no," he said, promptly: "not a bit. And if 1 had-" He checked himself and glanced through. the window; but Veronica rested her head more comfortably as if she did not share his impatience. _

!4A-iiid what did Mr. Talbot Denby say to make you so angry?" she asked as smoothly as before. Ralph coloured. "Oh, I don't know. He was rather trying—Then you saw us ?" he broke off, penitently. 'l'm sorry! "You • should endeavour to control your temper," said Veronica with sweet severity. "That's so," responded Ralph, with a meek- ness which would have astonished and gratified Talbot Denby. "And did you take the trout to—Mrs. Mason ? " asked Veronica after a pause. Ralph nodded, his brow clearing at the change to a subject free from embarrassment. "Yes, and she was very much obliged." "Very pretty girl, her daughter," remarked Veronica, soft as butter.
"Yes, oh, yes," agreed Ralph, without the slightest enthusiasm. "You don't think so!" she said, with wide open eyes of surprise.

-"Yea, oh, yea; at least I haven't thought. Oh, yes, I suppose she's pretty. To tell you the truth, I haven't noticed her particularly." A smile—was it of satisfaction ?—curved the beautiful lips and shone softly in the lovely eyes; but she said, as if disappointed with him: "I don't think you have very good taste." "Perhaps not," he admitted. "I don't admire that kind of face I suppose." "Really! And yet it is a very favourite one— fair, good complexion, with almost golden hair." "Yes, I know," he admitted, absently. "What type do you admire ? " she asked, with an affectation of casualness and indifference which a woman would have detected in a moment, but which was lost on Ralph, who, of course, pitmptly fell into the snare. "I like a girl with soft, dark hair, and grey eyes, violet eyes, and rather a pale face—what do you call it, old ivory ?—and long lashes—" He was gazing before him as if lost in the effort to word his mental picture, and did not see the colour that grew and ,grew in the "pale face of old ivory," or the smile that played about the beautiful lips. "Oh, that's a every common type," she said, contemptuously, but with a subtle sweetness in her voice.

Ralph started from his reverie and got up awkwardly. "I hear the carriage," he said. "They can't drive up to the door, I'm afraid." His face went red. But she shook her head as she raised herself. "No, no, I can walk, or hop, at any rate, if you will give me your arm "—for he was standing stiff with nervousness and no longer self - possessed, looking at her with a half-fearful embarrassment which, of course, restored her to her usual calm.
He held out his arm, and, putting her hand on it, she hopped to the door where her maid, Goodwin, met her, exclaiming in agonised accents
"Oh, Miss Veronica!" "Oh, it's 411 right," said Veronica. "Don't make a fuss."

"Take care! You'll strike your foot you can't hop into the carriage, cried Ralph, warningly. "I can't fly in," she retorted, pettishly. "Help me, please! " There was only one way of helping her; and, taking her in his strong arms once more, he lifted her in. Veronica sank back slowly, looking at him through her long lashes. "Thank you very much ! " she said, in a low voice.

Ralph drew back, feeling dazed and bewildered by the novel emotion and sensation which were throbbing within him. "Drive slowly ! " he said, hoarsely, but in a tone of command that would have been suitable to the Earl himself. Instinctively the coachman's hand went up to his hat, and he onry checked himself in time.
Ralph gazed after the carriage for a moment or two, then, drawing his hand across his brow as if to wipe away the mist that hung about his brain, he went into the hut.

A small, damp object lay on the floor beside the couch. It was Veronica's handkerchief. He picked it up and opened it, gazing at it vacantly, then he raised it to his lips. The touch of the cold, wet cambric brought him back to his senses.
"Oh, I'm mad!' he exclaimed with a harsh laugh, and he flung the handkerchief away from him.
But it seemed to reproach him mutely from where it lay, and presently, after he had paced up and down, glancing at it at each turn, he picked it up and thrust it impatiently into his breast-pocket.
(7'o he continued.)

MAGISTERIAL REFERENCES.

Before commencing the ordinary business at the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, the Chairman (Mr. H. Neild) said they had just lost a member of the Bench who was a man of great ability and who always acted in a fair and upright manner. He very much regretted the Colonel's death and he sympathised with the deceased gentleman's relatives and friends. Mr. Henry Greenall on behalf of the officials, said they much regretted the Colonel's death for they always found him to act like a gentleman both on the bench and as a citizen. Superintendent Ennion on behalf of the police said Colonel Ridgway was always ready to assist them as well as he could, and they felt his loss as much as any one. They sympathised with the deceased's relatives ~,and friends. . .

Mr. Steel on behalf of the solicitors practising in that court, said they always found Colonel Ridgway to be an efficient and conscientious magistrate and hd extended] his heartfelt sympathy to the relatives and friends.

div.head: BREWERY AMALGAMATION.
div.p: BREWERY AMALGAMATION.
Peter Walker and Son, Ltd., and Burton, Bell, and Co.

It is stated on good authority that negotiations have' recently passed between the Peter Walker and Son brewery companies and Messrs. Burton, Bell and Co., Wavertree, with a view to the business of the latter company being taken .over and amalgamated with the greater concern. There is reason to believe that these negotiations have proved successful, and that the purchase price is a quarter of a million pounds. The property of Messrs. Burton, Bell, and Co. consists of the Rose Brewery, Picton-road, Wavertree, wl. ere are also the offices of the firm, and a large number of licensed houses, mostly in the. East-end of Liverpool, including the districts of Wavertree, Old Swan, West Derby, Broadgreen, Knotty Ash, Roby, Huyton, &c., the total number of houses probably being about forty. The huge properties amalgamated under the name of Peter Walker and Son are owned by three limited ' liability companies. Peter Walker and Son, Warrington and Burton, Limited, was registered in 1890 to take over the brewery and wine and spirit businesses of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son and Messrs. MOnro and to., at Warrington and Liverpool, Messrs. A. B. Walker and Sons at Burton-on-Trent, and Messrs. A. B. Walker and Co. at Liverpool and other places. The I authorised capital of this company is £2,000,000, and power to issue .debentures for £1,000,000 has been utilised. In 189,1 the Peter Walker and Son Property Corporation, Limited, was formed with a capital of £222,500 to purchase licensed :Ind other properties then recently acquired by the senior com- pany, and £400,000 first mortgage debentures have been issued. Similarly in 1905 Peter Walker and Son Property Corporation (No. 2), Limited, was formed with a capital of £125,000 to take • over certain additional licensed and other property then acquired or to be acquired. In the case of the latter corporation power was obtained to issue £250,000 guaranteed four per cent. registered debenture stock, and the whole amount has been placed, £170,000 having been issued publicly in June, 1905. The head offices of the Peter Walker companies are situated in Duke-street, Liverpool.

div.head: REPENTING IN HASTE.
div.p: REPENTING IN HASTE.

A young woman of 19 was on Wednesday granted at Salford a separation from her husband, to whom she had been married seven months. It was explained that they were both quite willing to part, and that the husband had shown a disinclination to live with her.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
COUNCILLOR STOTT AND INFANTILE MORTALITY.
Proposed New School and Recreation Ground for Lovely-Lane.
BOWLING GREEN SUGGESTED FOR SAN KEY-STREET.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) presiding. There.. were also present :—The Deputy Mayor (Alderman Bolton) ; Aldermen A. Bennett, John Evans, W. J. Forshaw, D. Tinnion ; Councillors J. Ball, W. Benson, T. Burton, T. Chantler, W. Clegg, E. Cunnington, J. Dickenson, James Evans, L. Ellison, J. Hawthorn,J. Lord, J. J. Nield, J. Sankey, J. Skelland, T. S. Steel, J. Fulton-Smith, F. Stott, 0. Toole, 3.Wilkinson, W. J.Wilson ; Messrs. A.T.Hallaway (Deputy Town Clerk), Messrs. J. Fairhurst (Borough Treasurer), T. Longdin (Borough Surveyor), J. Deas (Water Engineer), W. S. Haddock (Gas Engineer), J. M. Murray (Director of Educaticon). POLICE SUPERANNUATION FUND.

The Committee recommended that George Henry Corbett and John Richard Malpas be appointed mem- bers of the Borough Police Force,they having served six months as probationers to the satisfaction of the Chief Constable.
Councillor Low) asked what were the terms with regard to superannuation upon which these constables were appointed. . The MA.YOR : The _Deputy Town Clerk says under

the old terms—after 25 years' service. Councillor LORD understood that these police constables could join the force at the age of 21, and after 25 years' service, at the age of 46, go on pension. If they would remember, two or three years ago this matter was brought before the Watch Committee and the Finance Committee, and a conference was arranged between the committees to take the superannuation scale into con- sideration, but the conference was never held. There was a general opinion that there should be some altera- tion made in the scale of pensions, and the terms of the engagement of new constables. He thought these" con- stables had been engaged with a view to extended ser- vice.
The MAYOR said they could not alter the rules. Constables bad to serve 25 years irrespective of their ages on joining the force. Councillor LORD: I think we can, if you will excuse me.
Later in the meeting the DEPUTY Tows CLERK said it was within the power of the Watch Committee to make an age limit below which constables could not retire without a medal certificate.
SALARY INCREASE FOR SUPERINTENDENT MONAGHAN.

The committee recommended that the salary of Detective-Superintendent Monaghan be increased to the sum of £2.00 per annum. Councillor LORD asked whether Superintendent Monaghan bad given any undertaking for further service. He understood he was entitled to go on the superannua- tion fund. The MAYOR: That is so. Councillor LORD: IS there any arrangement for an extension of service?
-.— The MAYOR : We have spoken to him, and we expect he will stay at least seven years. Councillor LORD: Is there any. definite agreement?

The MAYOR: No. We have discussed tTie matter with the Chief Constable, and he thinks the proposed plan the best. Councillor LORD said he agreed with paying' a man for the service he rendered, but still he thought the committee should enter into some tangible agreement with Superintendent Monaghan. The MAYOR: I will see if we can get one. We have taken his word so far. Councillor LORD: There is in reason why an agree- ment should notbe entered into. Alderman TINNION objected, and said he objected at the meeting of the committee, to compelling any man who had served a certain thud to enter into an agiee- ment to serve so many years longer. The position of Superintendent Monaghan was such that the committee did not wish to have theirhands tied by an lrrangement with him. It was just possible that circumstances might arise in which it would be much more difficult than at present to deal with the force in a proper way if they had a specific agreement with certain officials to serve for a fixed length of time. It was more than probable, in his opinion, that if Superintendent Monaghan retired from the office of superintendent,which be regarded as superfluous, would not be continued. The duties could probably be done by the Chief Inspector. But this was a !natter of discipline and routine in the force which might he left to the committee. While the committee were quite prepared to pay Superintendent Monaghan a sum equal to the services he had rendered to the town, and at the same time were prepared to con- tinue them, they were not prepared, as a Watch Com- mittee, to ask a man to say he would continue to serve them for so many years. It was always much more difficult to terminate a spEcial agreement than an ordinary agrument. While the Watch Committee expected that Superintendent Monaghan would give them his services, as in the past, for some years, there was no specific agreement, and in the opinion of the committee it was not desirable that there should be such an agreement. He thought the present policy a very sound one. Councillor BALL said after a payment of £3 a week to Superintendent Monaghan for nine years, the com- mittee gave him an increase of £4l per annum. He did not object tb the increase, personally, because he was quite sure Superintendent Monaghan had rendered valuable service to the town, but they must know that the police superannuation fund was not altogether upon a sound basis, and seriously required an examination by experts. He asked whether this increase had been given because the Watch Committee were tardily recognizing the services of the Superintendent or whether it was in order that he could come on an increased pension. If the latter were the explanation he thought it was a very reprehensible practice. They needed to be.yery careful how far they allowed increases, with the superannuation fund as it was. The MAYOR assured Councillor Ball that they were very careful with the superannuation fund.

div.head: minutes were then agreed to. KNIITSFORD-ROAD SCHEME. ALDERMAN BENNETT'S PROTEST.
div.p: The minutes were then agreed to. KNIITSFORD-ROAD SCHEME. ALDERMAN BENNETT'S PROTEST.

The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee resolved that the Town Clerk apply to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of the sum of £4,100 for the purchase of the Mersey Bedstead Company's premises-and the sum of 0,500 for the purchase of premises in Buttermarket-street from Messrs. Greensll. Whitley and Co., Ltd. The Committee, inspected the premises in Knutsford- road purchased from Mr. Edelsten and also the premises recently belonging to the Mersey Bedstead Company. With regard to the former it was suggested that as soon as the sanction of the Local Government Board had been given to the borrowing of the money the whole of the buildings should be demolished and the surplus land sold for lock-up shops or warehouses. With regard to the Mersey Bedstead Works the Committee were of opinion that all the buildings in front of the buiiding line should be demolished as soon as possible. Alderman BENNETT, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that personally he did not agree with the proposed use of the site of Mr. Edelsten's property. Llis.opinion was that they were making a mistake in attempting to erect any new buildings on that site. (Hear, hear.) If they took a long-sighted view of the position of Warrington, and legislated for the future instead of for immediate necessities,the proper course would be to make an esplanade from Warrington Bridge to Victoria Park. It would be a most attractive feature, and would give the town a distinction which not many towns possessed. Although they might for the moment enrich their coffers by erecting lock-up shops, which were almost sure to be ugly, and which would not bring in ,a large amount, he was quite sure they were acting in a foolish short-pighted way. He would prefer to see the site not built upon, but he knew he should not be able to carry the point, and, therefore, did not propose it. Councillor JAMES EVANS seconded, and the minutes were agreed to. THE NEW MEDICAL OFFICER.

CoUTICIIIOr EVANS, in proposing the adoption of the Health Committee's minutes, remarked that Dr. Hibbert had entered upon his work, and he had no doubt that the Council wished that his connection with the town might be a very peasant and a very long one. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BURTON seconded. INFANTILE MORTALITY.

COUNCILLOR STOTT AND ST. JOHN'S WARD. Alderman EVANS suggested that the Chairman of the committee might have some Mug to say about the question of infantile mortality in St. John's Ward. Councillor EVANS said he could only say that his attention had been called to a statement reported, in the Press as having been made by I Councillor Stott, and he thought at the time, and it was ' his present opinion, that it was a rather serious state- ment to make. During 1906 there, were 61 deaths under the age of one year in St. John's Ward. Of those 21 were deaths due to diarrhcea. He did not know what was in the mind of Councillor Sipa when he made the statement, but he wished to point out that going through the figures for 1906 it worked out that in the newly ' paved parts, and in the newly built parts of the ward the infantile mortality was rather the highest. It might sound strange butt in the area—which they would perhaps call slum area if they called any part of the ward slum area—bounded by Pilaw rs-brow, Nrginwick-street, Orfqkl- street, Fennel-street, Brick-street, and Lythgoes-lr

SCHOOL CHILDREN AND THE BATHS. ONE PENNY CHARGE SUGGESTED. Councill9r, STorr drew attention to the following resolution :—"That school children be allowad \to Use the second class plunge bath from the 19th July to the 19th August upon payment of id. each, on any day except Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 5' p.m.' and on Saturday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m." He asked whether that was the extent of the request to the Baths Committee. The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK said he thought that was SO. Councillor STOTT thought the privilege ought to be extended beyond the school holidays; they ought to teach boys to swim in school hours, and they ought also to encourage them after they had learned to swim to continue bathing. They could do that by admitting them all the year round at id. He moved that the minute be referred back with a view to extending the privilege for the other eleven months in the year. Councillor EVANS seconded. Alderman BOLTON pointed out that they had done as much as they could by allowing the boys this conces- sion,tbecause after the holidays the Education Com- mittee would again have the use, of the second class bath.

THE LEVEL CROSSING. The Committee also reported the receipt of a letter from the London and North-Western Railway Company stating that it was proposed to strengthen and partly re-constrnct the bridge carrying the railway over the river Mersey at Arpley Station, Warrington, that the re-construction would necessitate the widening of the bridge on the north side by one foot, and on the south side by about six feet, and that the widened portion would be of precisely the same span and headway as the existing bridge. The committee were of opinion that there Was noi objection to the proposals. Alderman BOLTON, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said they saw there was the usual letter—the usual dog-in-the-manger policy—from the Ship Canal Company, but as regarded the London and North- Western Railway Company they were always willing to help them all they possibly could. Councillor FULTO:sT-SMITH seconded. Alderman BENNErr suggested the time was opportune for considering whether it was not possible to get a larger scheme to obviate the nuisance of. pedestrians having to wait at the crossing. He was glad for his soul's salvation that he did not live at Stockton Heath, because how any man could retain his language in the bounds of moderation he did not know. Alderman TINNION said there was a footbridge. Alderman BENNETT : You cannot go over a footbridge in a tram. (Laughter.) Councillor LORD hoped they would call the attention pf Messrs. Fairclough and Admiral Nares to the widen- ing of the bridge; as they objected to the Warrington Bridge scheme and practically wrecked it. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: This is a one span bridge and our's is three. But no doubt Admiral Nares will get to know about it. The minutes were approved. CHEAP COAL. COUNCILLOR STOTT'S NOVEL PROPOSAL. Councillor SToTT, in alluding to the price paid for coal by the Water Committee, said he noticed the remarkable difference between the priee by the Corpora- tion and the private householder. It had been said that the average weekly consumption for domestic purposes was not less than 2cwt., and when they saw the Cortrora- don buying coal at 4s. per ton less than what the private consumer paid, the figures meant a great deal. ... . .
Alderman TES-SION said everyone agreed with what had been done by the Baths Committee. If they had a

There were about -14,600 inhibited houses in-the town, and he calculated tbat they were paying something like £15,000 a year more than they need to for coal. If the Corporation could buy coal for its own departments at 45. per ton less,whynot buy it for the whole community and stve the people £15,000? Some of them might say that was Socialism— Alderman BOLTON: It will cost 4s. a ton to deliver. Councillor STorr : The price includes delivery. The MAYOR: You are not speaking on the minute now. Councillor STorr : I am. The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK : You are making a wrong use of the minutes. Councillor STorT rejoined that he might be out of order' but he hoped the Council would pay heed to what he had said. Councillor FULTON-SMITTI said there was a big differ- ence bntween house coal and steam coal. Councillor LORD: We do not use steam coal at Bank House. The minutes were approved without further comment.

div.head: WORKMEN'S TRAM TICKETS.
div.p: WORKMEN'S TRAM TICKETS.

The Tramways Committee having received a letter from Councillor Wilson requesting tbat the holders of workmen's tickets be allowed to use the return 'half on any journey in or out at any time, the committee con- sidered the matter and were of opTion that .such an arrangement would lead to confusion and difficulties and could not see their way to adopt it. The MAYOR moved and Alderman FORSHAW seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor WILSON regretted that the committee could not accede to his request on behalf of a large number of workingmen: He asked that workmen should be allowed to use the return half of their tickets in a morning. For instance a man going from Latchford to Sankey Bridges ought to be able to use the return half on the Sankey Bridges route without having to buy another fresh ticket and part with 2d. on his morning journey. He moved that the minute be referred back. There was no seconder. The MAYOR said the committee had given the matter
consideration, and there were difficulties in the way. There was not a tramways company in Lancashire that gave as many privileges to workingmen as Warrington did.
The minutes were adopted. THE OLD POLICE COURT SITE.

• The General Purposes Committee recommended that tubs containing suitable shrubs be placed on the site of the old police premises, and that the Town Hall. Parks, and .134ths Committee be requested to attend to the same.

Councillor CLEGG said they were quite prepared to do their best with the plants when they brought them down, but he would like the , Chaitman of the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee to spare them a num- ber of tubs from the front of the Town Hall instead of keeping them waiting a year. (Laughter.) It would be a favour to that part of the town. A SCEIEHE FGR LOVELY-LANE. PROPOSED SCHOOL AND RECREATION

div.head: GROUND.
div.p: GROUND.

The General Purposes Committee resolved: "On the recommendation of the Open Spaces Sub-Committee that this committee co-operate with the Education Committee with regard to the proposed purchaae of a plot of land in Lovely-lane for the joint purposes of a school site and recreation ground." Councillor HA.WTITORN said he had not brought a petition in favour.of the proposal, but he believed one would have been readily signed by every ratepayer in the ward. That afternoon the site VMS being used by hundreds of children as a playground and it would be a distinct loss to the neighbourhood to allow it to pass into tne builder's hands. The district was being rapidly ! built up and there were very few vacant spaces left. It would be a wise policy on the part of the Corporation to close with the offer made in regard to this land. If the proposal was agreed tO by the Education Committee the new school would serve Bewsey and Whitecross Wards, in both of which he believed there was over- crowding of schools. The site was an excellent one, seven acres in extent. and there was not another so well suited to the purpose. The field was bounded on one side by the infectious diseases hospital and the Union Infirmary, and it was not desirable to build right up to those institutions with working class dwellings. It would be almost worth while for the Guardians to make the Corporation a grant to preserve an open space there. Whitecross Ward was one of the ' largest wards in the town and was one of the few i which had not a recreation ground. The MAYOR: It is one of the best looked after.
Councillor HA.WTITORN : I think we may take that as a compliment to those who represent it. (Laughter.) The MAltOlt : I meant it as such.

Councillor HAWTHORN said the site would be a very desirable acquisition and the Council would be acting in the best Interests of the town in securing it. Alderman BOLTON did not think they ought to build a school so near the hospital. If there was ally infec- tion the children would be the first to take it.

Councillor EVANS said he was quite 'expecting Alderman Bolton to say that. As the land was seven acres in extent the school could be built in a position sufficiently out of danger ofinfection and it would be considerably farther away from the hospital than some of the houses already were. It was the business of the Corporation to find ,recreation for children under proper conditions and sooner they set about it the better. • Councillor WILKINSON said he had had the site in view as a suitable one for a school for many years. He thought everyone in Warrington would agree that the land was admirable for the double purpose. The minutes were approved. INCREASES OF SALARY.
The following increases of salary were agreed to : Mr. F. W. Purse, chief sssistant engineer in the elec- tricity and tramways department, from £l7O to £2OO per annum,

Mr. A. T. Hallaway, deputy town clerk, from £213 to £250 per annum. Councillor CHANTLER, referring to Mr. Purse's advance, asked if these continual increases would affect the estimates. When a few months ago some members asked for an advance for the workmen they were told that the estimates were made up. The MAYOR said the increase would not come out of the rates. The rates had not paid a penny towards the electricity or tramways since the undertakings com- menced.

div.head: VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: THE VOLUNTEERS.
Last Day's Manoeuvres at Llanberis.

A number of the companies of the South Lancashire Brigade took part in a keenly-contested competition in the "attack "on Saturday, and after a very good con- test the prize for" the best coMpany "was awarded to the 6th Liverpool. The remainder of the brigade were exercised in a sham fight, and for this purpose the Ist South Lancashires and the 3rd Liverpools were sent off to occupy and defend a position on the heights above the camp reminiscent of Spion Kop, as described. On the face of it the position was one which could be defended with success against a very large force, but, in accordance with the "general idea," the attacking force, consisting of the 2nd South Lancashires and the 6th Liverpools, assailed and carried the position In facie of a number of machine guns and a volume of rifle fire, which in real warfare would have annihilated them. The brigade, in full war trim, marched seven miles to Carnarvon, presenting a very impos- ing eosemble as, with its three bands playing, and the men swinging along at a fine marching pace, it passed along through the peaceful Welsh countryside. A. large number of people had congregated in Castle- square, Carnarvon, in the hope of seeing the Volunteers march to the Castle, where, it was stated, they would have rations ; but they were greatly disappointed when it became known that the men had gone along a by-street in the outskirts of the town to the Carnarvon Park, which is about a mile from the town. The original intention was undoubtedly to go to the Castle, as the police had received instructions to so control the traffic as to facilitate the marching of the men through the principal streets to the historic building. The police had acted upon the instructions they received, and were holding themselves in readiness for any emergency, but they like the public, were destined to be disappointed, for the Volunteers came not that way,and their labour consequently was in vain. Naturally the question was asked, Why was the pro- gramme changed so suddenly? The reason was con- tained in a statement to the effect that the Volunteers would not be admitted into the Castle, which is Crown property, without the payment of 2d. per bead, which for over 2,000 men would have amounted to a consider- able sum. However, the townspeople were inclined to blame something or somebody for. having interfered with the original arrangements. After resting them- selves for an hour in the park, the men marched back to Llanberis by the same route exactly, their incoming and , outgoing being witnessed by only a few residents in ' the outskirts of the town.

The camp broke up on Sunday morning, entraining commencing as early as six o'clock. The Warrington Volunteers arrived home about noon and large‘ crowds witnessed the march to the Drill Hall. Notwithstanding the trying whether the men looked better for their week's stay under canvas.
