There are defections in the THE PASSING OF Liberal party. It is being LORD ROSEBERY. abandoned by one peer

after another. It was Lord SEFTCN on Tuesday. It is Lord ROSEBERY to-day. People swept their eyes with their hands when Lord SEFTON gathered up his mantle and departed. They wondered who he could be by any possibility. He announced his existence to the public by his resignation of a post in con- nection with which he had never been heard of, and his appointment to which had caused astonish- ment to all those who knew that such a post ex;sted. Lord SEFTON has done the one great thing of his life. He has reminded the -world of his existence. He disapproves of the measures of the Government which dragged him up out of obscurity. Which of these measures are most obnoxious to him he does not say. He possesses what used to be called " the grand manner." Like CORIOLANIIS, he banishes the Romans.

It is otherwise with Lord ROSHBERY. Lord MACAULAY before he had received that title spoke of Mr. GLADSTONE as "the rising hope of Toryism." It was one of the great historic misapprehensions, but Mr. GLADSTONE might himself have approved of it at the time. He did not then quite know whither his views were leading him, but as we all know at this time, they were always leading him towards the light. All men make mistakes, what- ever may be the amount of their inward illumina- tion, Mr. GLADSTONE made the mistake of designating Lord ROSEBERY as his successor. There is, we believe, no member of the Liberal party who did not desire to see Mr. GLADSTONE'S expectations realised. When Lord ROSEBERY did ' aueceed to the Premiership, he had not only the support Of the whole Liberal party behind him but its trust,its faith in him,its belief in the greatness of his future. Nothing that he had done,nothing that he had said until 1895 had stigF4ested that it would ever be possible for him to desert any of thaprinciples represented by him alike as Liberal Prime Minister and disciple of Mr. GLADSTONE. But there are some men who are like a bow, which is only tense so long as the hand of the bow- man is kept!upon it. Lord ROSEBERY is one of these. He" wilted " when the strong hand of Mr. GLADSTONE was removed.

It seems to have strink him that England might be led in other directions than those which had been marked out by his groat predecessor. Point by point he abandoned the Liberal positions. Of late he has been sitting in the House of Lords on what are known as the " cross benches." On the last occasion on which he spoke before Tnesday he went over to the place occupied by Lord LANMDOWNE, speaking, that is to say, from the Tory benches, but with a sort of apology for doing so. After his Tuesday's speech he ought to abandon thei cross benches acd wholly identify himself with the opponents of the Government. That is the only clearly honest course that is possible to him. We bid him a reluctant fare- well. He is a man of that kind of ability which amounts almost to genius, but as a Liberal-- whatever he may become as a Conservative—he is a spent force in politics.

WHITE CITY, MANCHESTER.

I The White City in Manchester has been conceded to be one of the most accessible amusement places in Eng- land. The beautiful old Botanical Gardens are really transformed into a fairyland of delight. The Manage- ment are showing that nothing is too good for their public and are sparing no pains or expense to make this the summer resort par excellence. The very best entertainment obtainable has been secured, as is seen by their attractive programme. Together with the many attractions of concessionaires the Management have provided many free entertainments and exhibitions such as the Free Circus, the Water Pantomime, the Log Rolling, etc., etc., the engagement of all the Best Bands in England who give free Concerts every afternoon and evening. The spacious Ball Room is very popular, so also is the Skating Rink. Hales Tours of the World, that ever instructive and educational entertainment, is receiving a good share of the patronage it deserves. The same can be said of the Water Chutes, Mystic Rivers, Figure 8, Dragon Slide, etc., etc.

It has frequently been A HEAVY noticed and remarked that OBITUARY, one death among the public men of a town is quickly followed by others. Last week Warrington was shocked by the news of the sudden death of Colonel Ridgway. Hardly had this respected officer been laid to rest in the quiet churchyard at Daresbury, before the town, and particularly the Catholic section of the community, was stricken with the sad news that Father McGrath, recently of St. Mary's Church, Latchford, had passed away on Wednesday at West Kirby. On Thursday came a blow that had been feared, for the Rev. E. J. Willcocks, the greatly respected Master of the Grammar School, succumbed to the painful illness from which he had been suffering so long. In another column we publish a brief sketch of the public career of these two last-named gentlemen, but we should like to express here our regret at the calling away of two such useful and worthy men. Both com- manded a large measure of public respect and affection. The Rev. E. J. Willcocks in particular, has left his mark on the life of the town. During the thirty-seven years in which he was connezted with the Boteler Grammar School many of the best of Warrington's sons passed through his hands, and his influence unquestionably went far towards the correct moulding of the character of these youths. Tile" old boys" of this long period—those whom death has not already claimed—will mourn deeply the loss of so true a friend and master as Mr. Willcocks or " Dick " as he was affectionately termed. His filmily's sorrow they will, in common with the townspeople, respectfully and sympathetically share.
If we were asked what we

THE BIGGEST AND thought would be the BEST IMPROVEMENT. biggest and best improve- ment in Warrington we should outline a comprehensive scheme for rebuild- ing Warrington Bridge, widening the approaches to it, and doing away with the Wilderspool cross- ings! The idea has been talked of before, but its magnitude appalls most of our city fathers. There is one, however, who can grasp it fully, but still remains unable to make it appear more than a roseate dream to his fellows in the Council. We refer to Alderman Bennett, who took' occasion on Tuesday to point out that the proposed alterations to the Arpley rail- way bridge by the London and North-Western RAilway Company provided an opportunity for opening the subjeat and getting rid of the cross- ings. If we could only do this much it would be a vast cenvenience to the users of Wilderspool-road Alderman Bennett said" he did not know how ' any man could be stopped at the Crossings and retain his language within the bounds of modera- tion." W 3 would add "hear, hear" most fervently. The Crossings are a " cussed " nuisance to the people of Warrington. They even lower the dignity of the town. Are we for ever and a day to endure the blocking of one of our busiest approaches by an antediluvian railway crossing? It seems so, unless the flying machine supersedes the railway system. Is such an improvement scheme beyond the capacity of our Corporation and the resources of the town? We should like to know.
The question of bringing THE GAS OFFICES, the clerical staff of the Gas

Department under one roof with the other municipal offices was again raised at the Council meeting. Councillor Hawthorn's remarks were quite to, the point and he put the case in a nutshell when he said " Tao present system had several objections to it. It caused unnecessary duplication, it involved the payment of a larger staff than necessary, and it inconveni- enced the ratepayers. The Borough collector sent his assistants with rate papers to nearly every house, and immediately following were emissaries from the Gas Office. Then the ratepayer had to pay one account at Bank House and another at Mersey-street." It will be remembered by many of our readers that Mr. E. England, one of the elective auditors for the Borough, in his report last year drew attention to the unsatisfactory system at present in vogue and suggested the merging of the account collecting at the Gas Offices with the other collecting depart- ments at Bank House. It is manifest that a considerable economy could be effected by the centralisation of offices, bat the greatest boon would be to the individual ratepayer who is at present put to such unnecessary and periodical in convenience. Thereare difficulties in the way, doubtless,and probably some prejudices to overcome but the question is one that demands the serious attention of the Council. On Tuesday it was only raised on a side issue. The best course, it seems to us, would be to appoint a special Sub-Committee to consider the whole scheme and report.

"No doubt Lord Rosebery would resent any compari- son b etween himself and Mr. Victor Grayson, the Socialist member for the Colne Valley, and yet there is a superficial resemblance, for they are both leaders who do not lead when there is any trouble to be appre- hended."—" Christian World." * *,*
Sir W. S. Gilbert has written one limerick, and as might be expected, it is inimitably and subtly humor- ous. It reads :
There was a young man of St. Bee's Who was fearfully stung by a a Wasp When I asked ! does it sting ! He replied yes it does! But I thought at first it was a Hornet. 0 • *

The Methodists are extremely active and provident in the arrangements which they make for looking after the members of their own communion. They have just established an emigration league, the object of which is to advise and assist Methodists whc may be going abroad, whether to the colonies, the United States, or to foreign countries. The league will do what it can to bring such emigrants into contact with Methodists in the country to which they are going. The example is one which might be followed by other bodies.

The servant of a Corporation is usually considered a fortunate individual, and not without reason. You rarely hear of him being discharged, and never of his salary being reduced. On the contrary he gets regular increases without much difficulty. At Tuesday's Council meeting, three official obtained a "rise "of £3O, £35, and £44 per year respectively. In the latter case the increase was one of about 30 per cent. The Corporation is a generous paymaster. *

Marie Corelli, the unsparing critic of man, was recently asked by a perhaps too-familiar friend the reason why she did not marry. "Well, you know," was the reply, "I am a feminist." " But," insinuated the inquirer, who was a feminist of the old school, "don't you think it woulcl be nice to have a man about the house ?" "No," was the decisive response. "I have three pets at home, which, together, answer the same purpose. I have a dog which growls all the morning, a parrot which swears all the afternoon, and a cat which comes home late at night." * * *

In our issue of last Saturday we referred to the dangerous character of St James'-street from the Bedstead Works to Warrington Bridge, and expressed the hope that, now the property had been acquired, the widening of the street would not be long delayed. As if to emphasize our remarks, the very same day a cyclist had a miraculous escape from death at this very spot. He skidded on the tram lines—which are usually kept wet —and fell in front of a tramcar which carried him along for a short distance. Instead of being crushed to death he escaped with a few bruises and shock.

Stockton Heath has for several years rejoiced in a flower show of its own, and so much enterprise has been displayed by the villagers that the exhibition has assumed quite respectable proportions. Notwith- standing the wretched season, Saturday's show was highly creditable, the display of plants and flowers being tasteful and attractive. Lady Brooke, who performed the opening ceremony, delivered an admir- able speech in which she advocated gardening as a pastime for all and showed how success entirely depended upon the care bestowed upon each plant. The pity of it is that so many people have no gardens to cultivate, but efforts are being made to induce the dwellers in crowded streets to brighten their surround- ings with window plantsxand*boxes of flowers. Alderman Bolton is becoming quite a reformed character—one can almost detect a hitherto-unlooked for mellowness in his disposition. It will be remem- bered that when the Victoria Park municipal bowling green was being discussed, the chairman of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee was violently opposed to the project. He even went so far as to say that grass would not grow in Warrington, obviously forgetful of the fact that even orchids grow within the borough. On Tuesday he was quite enthusiastib about the provision of a bowling green behind Garven place, and even generous about bathing. Said he, "they would let everyone have free baths if there was sufficient accommodation." The advocates of bowls and baths in the open-air ought to pursue the Alderman while he is in this complaisant frame of mind

0 An important scheme for Whitecross Ward was introduced to and sanctioned by the Town Council this week. The General Purposes Committee is to co-operate with the Education Committee in the pur- chase of the seven-acre site between Lovely-lane and the Union buildings for the purposes of a school and recreation ground. Whitecross Ward is one of the biggest and most progressive districts in the borough, and the need not only of increased school accommoda- tion, but of a playground for the large juvenile popula- tion, is pressingly felt. There should be an open space in every Ward, but the congestion of property prevents the provision of such a " lung" in some quarters. Here, however, the land is open, and the opportunity of securing it for future generations of children is so good, that it would be folly to miss it. * * *

Thanks to the success of the amateur opera tic per- formances, the Warrington Musical Society is in a sound financial position, but it is to be regretted that last season there was again a loss on the concerts. The Society does its best to educate the public taste to high-class music, but unfortunately it does not meet with the support it deserves. Why, it is difficult to say, for the members spare no trouble to place excel- lent programmes before their patrons. A sugges- tion made at the annual meeting might, if acted upon, result in larger audiences—to have six- penny seats at every concert in order to cater for the working classes. The programme for next season is an ambitious one, for it includes Sir Edward Elgar's "Dream of G-erontitis "—a difficult work, the produc- tion of which will be looked forward to with interest. A new departure will be the performance of "The Messiah "on Boxing Day, and the season will con- elude with Gounod's " Faust."

* Councillor Stott sprung a little surprise on the Council on Tuesday. Speaking to the minutes of the Gas Committee, he drew attention to the remarkable difference between the price paid for coal by the Cor- poration and by the private householder. The Council listened attentively. The Councillor advanced an illuminating suggestion. He found the difference was about 4s. per ton in favour of the Corporation as a buyer, and he calculated that the 14,000 house- holders in Warrington were paying something like £15,000 a year more than they need to pay for coal. Still the Council was attentive, but when Councillor Stott suggested that if the Corporation cotild buy coal at 4s. per ton less than the individual it might as well buy for everybody and save the community the £15,000, then came the laugh and the look of surprise on the faces of the members. Some were serious and others " scoffing rude." Before Councillor Stott could be interrogated as to the significance of the difference between steam coal and house coal he was ruled out of order. It still remains an open question whether he was serious or indulging in a kind of Socialistic joke, but the ideal of municipalising the supply of coal at the expense of the co aloxvners was good.

Another Drowning Fatality. Alfred Nanson, aged 26, 128, Evelyn-street, was found drowned in the Sankey and St. Helens canal on Thursday evening at 7.45. An inquest will be held.
PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LA.NOASHIRE.—AdVt.

Licensing Transfers. The following licences were transferred by the magistrates at the Borough Court on Monday : —from John James Booth to John Barnes, off-licence, 6, Bewsey-road ; from E. A. Hollingworth to Peter Lawless, beerhouse, the Borough Arms; from W. Jones to Clement Melbourne, off-licence, 11, Brick- street; from J. T. Collins to Sarih Skelton, off-licence, 9, Aikin-street. GARDEN TENTS.—Tennis, Croquet, and other out- door sports.—J. S. GARLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. False Alarm. At about 3.35 on Sunday afternoon John Mannion who resides in Wellington-street, was passing the warehouse of Messrs. Stanley Carter and Gandy when he observed smoke and sparks issuing from one of the windows. The alarm was given and the fire brigade turned out, but on their arrival they found out that the smoke and sparks which were stilf coming through the window were caused by the back draft from the boiler fire. There were men working in the place at the time.

Poor Children's Summer Camp. The last contingent of boys (103) returned home last night. We are pleased to note that several huts have been taken by Warrington people who aye spending their holidays at Prestatyn, but there are still a number vacant. No inquiries have to be made in Warrington if any person desires to occupy one. Subscriptions are required to support the excellent work of the camp. They can be sent to the hon. secretary, Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, Horsemarket-street, or to the hon. treasurer, Mr. J. A. Ransom.

J. S. GARLAND, Ironmimger, Bridge-street, Wei- rington.—Advt. Bostock and Worobwell's Menagerie. Considerable interest centred in the visit of this old-established menagerie to Warrington on Tuesday and Wednesday and there were many visitors to the tent which was pitched on the Wilierspool meadows. The collection exhibited was an exceptionally fine one and included many rare specimens. A giant clog and a very diminutive pony formed a unique feature. The thrilling exploits in the cages of wild beasts appealed most to the multitude, lions, bears, wolves, and leopards being put through remarkably clever performances. An exceedingly well-trained elephant also provided an interesting entertainment. FARM-FED FAT BAcoN,sd.per lb.at ASEILEY'S.—Advt. Beautiful Warrington Society. Attention is called to the second annual exhibition of the Society which will be held in the Drill Hall on Saturday, 31st August. The exhibition will be opened by Mrs. Lyon at 2.30 p.m. A splendid orchestra, under the conductorship of Ur. Tom Boothroyd, wat give selections of music. The flowers and plants grown in the town will be well worth an inspection. The judging of the outside exhibits will shortly take place. Although the present season has not been a good one for gardens, the entries for this class show an advance on last year. Many pretty effects have been attained, and the judges for these classes, Messrs • W. H. Woodcock and J. Ryan will have no easy taelr•

THE ACCOUNTS.

- The accounts were submitted by Mr. Atkin who took 1 over the duties of treasurer on the death of Mr. ; Reynolds. The total receipts from the concerts were , £2“l 9s. 4d. The items included: Subscriptions, £BO , 1 108. 6d.; members' subscriptions, £5O 15s. Od. • sale of 1, tickets and programmes, £9B ss. 2d. The first concert showed a loss of £3B 9s. Bd., and the second a loss of 11 16s. id., and the third, at which there was no pro- fessional aid, a profit of £l5 us. 4d., which left a loss for the season of £29 14s. sd. On the general account there was a balance at the bankers of £4O Gs. 3d. The subscriptions to the concerts for the past season had been totally inadequate and the money taken at the doors was not what it ought to be. The subscriptions totalled £BO 10s. 6d. as against £lOB 2s. last year. There was therefore a great deal wanting in that respect and the sale of tickets should also be increased. On the proposition of Mr. NEWCOMBE, seconded by Mr. PRICE, the balance sheet was adopted. The CHAIRMAN proposed and Mr. GOUGH seconded, a vote of thanks to Mr. Atkin, and it was carried unani- mously. ELECTION OF OFFICERS. The following officers were re-elected :—President, Mr. J. Charlton Parr ; Vice-presidents, the Mayor, Messrs. Ziba Armitage, W. E. Atkin, A. H. Crosteld, M.P., James Fairclough, John Fairclough, R. T. Fair. dough, F. A. Frost, W. N. Hutchings, F. Monks, J. Monro, C. E. Parker, Roger C. Parr, Robert Pierpoint, H. Roberts and John White, with the addition of Captain Crosfleld ; Treasurer, Mr. W. E. Atkin ; Secretary, Mr. C. P. Gough • Committee: Messrs. Bond, Bibby, Johnson, Knowles, Newcombe, Price, Scotson, Silcock, Wallington and Whitfield. NEXT SEASON'S PROGRAMME. Mr. CROSSLEY then alluded to the coming season's programme. The dates of the concerts were :—Tuesday, November 26th, "Dream of Gerontius " ; Thursday, December 26th, the "Messiah " ; and Tuesday, March 3rd, Gounod's " Faust." The Boxing Di,y performance of the " Messiah" was an innovation which had proved highly successful in other towns. Business people who could not attend a concert on Saturday evening would have the opportunity of hearing the work. He would like a special effort to be made to increase the subscription list. It was gratifying to find how the members' subscriptions kept up and they had more new members last year than they had, so far as he remembered, at any time in the history of the Society. So long as the Society continued its work on the present high standard, it had something to be proud of, but they wanted to arouse more public interest. He considered the "Dream of Gerontius "to be the finest work written by a British composer. Its magnitude was such that a very large orchestra would be required and that would entail considerable expense. For the first concert they bad engaged Miss Gertrude Lonsdale (soprano), Mr. Alfred Heather (tenor), and Mr. Fowler Burton (bass), and for the second concert, Miss Esta D'Argo (soprano), Mr. Charles Saunders (tenor), and Mr. Albert Garcia (bass). The contralto had not yet been engaged. The practices would begin on September 17th. Mr. NEWCOMBE suggested that in order to gain the inoreased support of the working-classes, there should be Gd. seats at every concert. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the :meeting.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
"A BIG RASCAL"

Thomas Pye, one of the most notorious characters in St. Helens. was on Tuesday sentenced to six months' hard labour on a charge of aggravated assault on May Edwards, a girl of sixteen, on Friday night last. The girl was going along Mill-street at twenty minutes to eleven on an errant], when she was pounced upon Pye. who was in an entry by the side of the street. The girl was treated in a most scandalous manner. The Chief Constable said it would be difficult to meet a bigger rascal than Pye. He had been been convicted sixty-one times, and was a very dangerous man. GAME TRESPASS AT ST. HELENS. Michael Farrell and James Povey, of Windle City were charged at St. Helens, on Tuesday with game trepass near Moss Bank. Mr. E. W. Swift prosecuted for Colonel Richard Pilkington, and said that on Wednesday, the 24th ult., James Craven, the game- keeper of Windle Hall, saw these two men with a dog in some fields through which a footpath ran. Later a net was found on the gate.—Povey said they had been tried for this once.—The Chairman: What do you mean by that ?—Povey : He took us to Rainford ' in front of Colonel Richard Pilkington and young Mr. Norman, and they told him to let us go.—The game- keeper said he did not know until afterwards that a net had been used. It was found by Mr. Glover, the farmer, who was present, and assisted in the capture of 1 the men.—Both men were fined ss. and Bs. costs.

div.head: COSTLY SPREE.
div.p: A COSTLY SPREE.

GLASS MANIJFACT LTRER'S CLAIM FOR DAMAGES On Monday, at the St. Helens Police Court, Ernest Worth, of 45, Doulton-street, was charged with neglect- ing his work at the glass works of Mrs. Mooney, and causing damages to the amount of £2o.—Mr. Webster, who appeared for complainant, stated that defendant was employed as a teaser at the complainant's works, and on Saturday, the 20th of July, he went to work at half-past five. He ought to have remained until he was relieved on the Sunday morning, but on the Sunday, morning the furnaces were found to be ou,t, and defend- ant was nowhere to be found. Subsequently he was seen by one of the workmen, to whom he admitted that he had got drunk and left the place. The furnaces were considerably damaged, and more than a week elapsed before they could be got right again. In conse- quence about 30 workmen were thrown out of work.— Defendant admitted he was drunk, and said the foreman , saw he was drunk and should have sent bun away from 1 the work.—The defendant was ordered to pay £lO. A COSTLY MISTAKE.

Henry Powell, an able-bodied young man, of Parr- street, was dealt with by the St. Helens magistrates, on Tuesday, on three charges of drunkenness and assault. Henry John Morecroft, who formerly held the licence of the Batb3 Hotel, Warrington New-road, said the licence had been extinguished, and the house had been converted into a shop. About half-past three on Mon- day afternoon Powall walked into the house and demanded drink. He could not believe that there was no drink to be had there, and used very foul language. After a good deal of trouble Powall vias told to go away, but refused, and at once attacked Morecroft. He was pushed into the street, but returned and rushed at Mr. Morecroft again. After being struck on the nose Morecroft violently rejected the man. He then stripped off in the street, and danced up and down the road challenging Morecroft to fight, until Police-constable Swift came up. When the officer was putting on the handcuffs Powall butted him several times and struck him. Al tram conductor then rendered the officer assist- ance, and Powall was looked up. The bench fined
The Examiner, Saturday; August 17, 1907
Powall 10s. and cost for drunkenness, 20s. and costs for assaulting the officer, and twenty-eight days for assault- ing Morecroft, the full alternative being ten weeks' hard labour.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON,
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON,
THE RAINFALL.

The rainfall at Newton Cemetery for the month of July measured 3.47in5., bringing up the total for the three months of May, June and July to a fractional point under 123-ins., a record for these months, June having seen the heaviest fall for 37 years. Rain fell on 14 days in July, the heaviest occurring on the 21st- 85ins. The total up to the end of July was 19.54in5., though the first four months did not produce 7ins.

BOWLING. The Thursday team of the Newton-le-Willows Bowling Club had a most enjoyable outing last week to Tuebrook to play the Marlborough Bowling Club, who proved to be the victors by 42 points on the singles, and owing to the rain the doubles were abandoned. The green was in perfect condition, the surroundings delightful, and the social element was a credit which the Newton team hope to repay on the return visit on Thursday next.

div.head: NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.

- - - - At these Sessions last Thursday before Messrs. T. J Gillespie (chairman), F. Wood, and W. Collingwood, Patrick Peppard was summoned for having illegally removed certain goods from 90, Athol-street, Earles- town.—F. J. Ball deposed that on Sunday morning, July 14, the defendant removed all his furniture from the house, to avoid destraint for £5 195., rent due.—Defend- ant said his wife and children did the flitting; he knew nothing about it. He also denied owing the rent, and produced a rent book to show that he only owed about 30s.—Plaintiff said that was for this year only ; the rent was in the last two years, but the rent books for those years were not in Court.—The case was adjourned for the books to be produced, defendant saying plaintiff admitted, though he had not brought them in Court. Alfred Broster and William Wharmby were summoned for gaming by playing at pitch and toss in Back Wood- street, Earlestown, and fined 58. and costs each. Thomas Ball, for being drunk while in charge of a horse and cart in High-street, Newton, was fined ss. and costs; James Travis and John Lythgoe, 2s. 6d. each, and Michael Dillhoyd 55., for drunkenness ; Mary Ellen Lowe ss. for using foul language.
EARLESTONIA:sIS IN CANADA. A WOMAN POLITICIAN.
I M

A copy of the "Toronto News," recently to hand contains an interview which runs into more than three columns and is embellished with a photograph of Mr. Edwin Worsley, late of Sankey-street, Earlestown, but who now resides at 92, Armstrong-avenue, Toronto. The nature of the interview will be readily guaged if we set out the headings, which like the remaining letter- press, are in real Transatlantic style. Thus— MRS. E. WORSLEY, THE POLITICIAN.
AN, INTERESTING TALK WITH A RED-HOT WOMAN- LABOUR SOCIALIST.

div.head: RECENTLY FROM ENGLAND.
div.p: RECENTLY FROM ENGLAND.
HOW WOMEN FOUGHT AND WON IN NEWTON, LANCASHIRE-A STRIKING CHARACTER.

The article states that " Mr. Worsley's enthusiasm for politics is mild compared with his wife's ; she is a red- hot Labour-Socialist." She tells the interviewer how the Newton Division was won for Labour, and that Earlestown thought it had a winner in J. A. Seddon. As Mrs. Worsley put it: "We knew our man had his head screwed on the right way." Mrs. Worsley was elected treasurer of the Women's Campaign Fund and by dint of hard work they collected a large sum of money. As a girl she lived in another part of the constitu- ency, the daughter of a Tory father. Says Mrs. Worsley: "The people that had grown up with !me hissed me when they saw me collecting for a Labour candidate." The reporter adds. "There was no bitterness in her tone. She forgave, in the joy of victory." Then the article goes on to say the employes of the manufacturers had not the liberty of a political conscience. They had to pretend to vote blue, and were dingy-donged to the polls wearing the ribbons. A miner who refused to vote a certain way was afterwards given a job where he could not earn his salt and had to give it up, and this was cited as an instance of what4the Labour Party had to put up with Mrs. Worsley bad some very strong things to say about Mr. Chamberlain, John Burns, the Liberal Party, the King's children, and the House of Lords. The report concludes " There's nothing of the public-platform, speechifying, fiery, unwomanly women's rights about Mrs. Worsley. She does her work in her home, looking after the needs of the household, 9n d in her spare time she listens, and reads, and thinks for herself. As she said 'good time' she took up her children to put them to bed." The Canadian journalist was so struck with the Newton Election literature that for the edification of his readers he prints copious extracts.

div.head: WARRINGTON BURIAL SOCIETY.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON BURIAL SOCIETY.

The members of the above Society met at the British Workmen's Public-house, Horsemarket-street, on Monday to celebrate the 36th anniversary of the estab- lishment of the Society. The attendance of the members was very good, the meeting being presided over by the president, Mr. Thomas Baskerville, jun., who was sup- ported by the vice-president, Mr. Joseph Ashton; treasurer, Mr. James Parr ; trustees Messrs. Peter Edgar, William Eckersley, James Gresly ; auditor. Mr. Joseph Adams ; general secretary, Mr. Lawrence Weir, and others. The CHAIRMAN in his address expressed his thanks to all for the honour which he had the privilege to possess during the past twelve months as President of the Warrington Burial Society. He said it had been a pleasure for him to preside at the various meetings in connection with the Society and to associate himself with their capable officers and most energetic committee who had done all in their power to assist him and make his duties as light as possible for which he felt very grateful. He con- gratulated,the members on the success and the steady progress which the Society had made during the year, having placed considerably over £2OO to their capital during the year, which is very creditable indeed, and a fact which he felt sure every member present would feel proud of. The GENERAL SECRETARY presented his annual balance sheet, which showed that the Society's funds now amounted to £3,497 4s. 110., compared with £3,260 12s. 7311. for the year previous, a gain of £236 12s. 44. The numerical condition was 1,464 com- pared with 1,435 last year. The report further showed that the Society had paid away in death claims £45 10s., compared with £6B ss. the previous year, and that they had invested in the Corporation, and upon mortgage almost £3,000. The Secretary, in conclusion briefly pointed out that during the last fourteen years they had made a gain of £2,417 15s. 78., and felt certain that under the new rules these gains would keep increas- ing. The extension of the age limit had during the year proved a success, and he urged the committee and collectors to make every effort in bringing those benefits before that portion of the public who bad not already made a provision through any other Insurance Society as each were endeavouring to do their best for their members. (Applause.) The AUDIToRS reported that the accounts and register kept aby the General Secretary, and also the books of the Treasurer and collectois had been examined, and they had pleasure in certifying the same to be correct and satisfactory. div.head: CRAWFORD'S
div.p: CRAWFORD'S
CREAM
CRACKERS.
LOCAL OBITUARY.
The Rev. E. J. Willcocks.

With deep regret—which will be shared by all our readers—we record the death of the Rev. E. J. Willcocks, M.A., headmaster of the Warrington Grammar School, who passed away at his residence, Heathfield, Latchford, at nine o'clock on Thursday morning after a prolonged illness. The end was not unexpected, for Mr. Willcocks had long been in a precarious condition, but when the sad news became generally known it occasioned profound sorr.m, for few gentlemen were more widely esteemed. A career of devoted service in the cause of educa- tion is thus closed. Mr. Willcocks, who was a son of the late Mr. Roger Willcoeks, of Teignmouth, was born in that town on March 11th, 1847. He was educated at first privately, but at the age of 16 he entered Trinity College, Dublin, where he soon gave proof of his genius for mathematics by gaining distinctions at three different terminal examina- tions in that branch of science. In 1865 he proceeded to Cambridge and read, with Mr. W. Besant as private tutor, for an open scholarship. He succeeded in winning a senior mathematical scholarship at St. Catherine's College, and 'after a brilliant University career he graduated as Wrangler, taking his B.A. degree in 1869 and MA. in 1872. He was ordained deacon by the Bishop of Chester in 1870 and priest in 1871, and in 1869-70 acted as assistant master at Cheam School, Surrey, coming to Warrington in the last-named year as second master of the Boteler Grammar School, which position he held until 1880, when he was appointed headmaster in succession to the Rev. 0. H. Cary who had retired after a long and very successful tenure of office. Under Mr. Willcock's direction, the school has made very gratifying progress, many of the boys having attained considerable distinction in the world of art, science and commerce. The Board of Education reports on the work] done have been of a highly complimentary character and several years ago the curriculum was altered and the school was much improved structurally, in order that it might be brought under Government control and a Government grant earned. Latterly the controlling influence in the school has passed into the hands of the Warrington Education Committee and a scheme of scholarships has been arranged in order that the working classes may have a greater share in the benefits of the institution. Mr. Willcocks was held in great respect and affection by the boys and exercised a marked influence of good in their lives. It was always a source of pride to him when his pupils brought credit to the old school and at the annual Speech Day gathering he used to recount the list of successes with obvious pleasure and satisfaction. Mr. Willcocks was curate of Orford from 1870 to 1878 and was much esteemed by the parishioners. Since he became headmaster, he fre- quently assisted in the conduct of the services at the Warrington Parish Church. At one time he took a prominent part in conducting the science classes instituted by the Corporation, paying special attention to the mathematical section. When the Education Act of 1902 came into operation, Mr. Willcocks was co-opted a member of the Warrington Education Committee and his knowledge and experience proved of great service to the committee. He eventually resigned the position but never ceased to take an interest in local educational affairs. In 1874 Mr. Willcocks married Miss Edith Taylor, daughter of The late Mr. Thomas. Taylor, of Kersal Bank, Manchester, by whom he is survived. Great sympathy is felt with the widow and family (two sons and one daughter) in their bereavement. Mr. Willcocks' kindly and genial disposition gained for him the affectionate regard of all who enjoyed his friendship and his death is sincerely lamented. . The funeral will take place at 12 o'clock noon on Monday at Grappenhall Church.

div.head: Rev. J. McGrath.
div.p: Rev. J. McGrath.

Roman Catholics in Warrington and district and many members of other denominations will deeply regret to hear of the death of the Rev. James McGrath, for five years priest in charge of St. Mary's Church, Latchford, who passed away at West Kirby on Wednesday after a long illness. The deceased, who was 46 years of age, was educated at Ushaw College and his firstjcuracy was at St. Werburgh'st Birkenhead. From thence he went to Morley Hall, Shropshire. In 1900 he was appointed to St. Mary's Mission, Latchford, and here he d;d a splendid work which will be a lasting memorial to him. He was greatly beloved by his flock for be was of a sympathetic nature and ever ready to help them. The great project to which he set his band was the erection of a new church and this was accomplished, a handsome edifice being built at a cost of £7,000. Two years ago his health broke down, and he relinquished the work at Latch- ford, and was sent to Lisbon in the hope that the change would benefit him. On returning to England he stayed at Blackpool for some time, and two months ago he went to West Kirby, where he died. He was a devoted priest, and did a good work, and many in Warrington will cherish his memory. The funeral took place at Birkenhead yesterday. A solemn requiem was celebrated at St. Werburgh's, Birkenhead, in the presence of a large congregation. The Rev. Father Chambers officiated at the church, and also at the graveside. The chief mourner was the deceased's brother, Mr. John McGrath. There were present from Warrington : The Rev. Father Roche, Messrs. Peter Bate and George Bibby.; Mrs. Walter Wallington, Miss Wells and Miss Caldwell IFather McGrath was buried in the grave of his old friend, Provost Baguet, in Flaybrick Hill Cemetery, Birkenhead,

div.head: Mr. Arthur Walker,
div.p: Mr. Arthur Walker,

We regret to record the death • at Torquay of Mr. Arthur Walker, fourth son of the late Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, Bart. The deceased gentleman had long been in a delicate state of health and had travelled abroad a great deal in the hope of recuperating. He was not personally connected with Warrington, but all his brothers are members of the firm of Messrs. Peter

Walker and Son Limited, the well-known brewers, Sir Peter Walker, Bart., being the chairman, and Colonel J. Reid Walker and Colonel W. Hall Walker, ALP., managing directors. The deceased gentleman was not identified with the firm. The funeral took place at Torquay yesterday. As a mark of respect the flags at the King-street and Dallam breweries were displayed at half-mast.

div.head: APPRENTICES AND THE ARMY.
div.p: APPRENTICES AND THE ARMY.
Singular Case at Warrington.
MR. A. H. GROSFIELD, M.P. En Route for Switzerland.
LETTER ON CURRENT LEGISLATION. The Lords and the By-Elections.
Sir,—May I before starting for Switzerland send a few notes on some very important Bills we are sending to the House of Lords.

First of all there is the English Land Bill, a measure which was not seriously resisted by the , Opposition, who refrained from voting against its Second Reading. In a word, it is, I think, a very fine feather in Mr. Lewis Harcourt's cap. Then we have the Evicted Tenants' Bill, one which will, I am sure, have the approval and support of my Irish friends in Warrington.

There is also the Bill f3r the separate valuation of Land in Scotland, which has the approval of almost all the local authorities in these islands, and a similar measure was actually carried on Second Reading by a majority of more than 200 in the last Tory House of Commons. Next we come to

div.head: SCOTTISH LAND BILL,
div.p: THE SCOTTISH LAND BILL,

a measure which has been vehemently opposed in committee, and which is much disliked by some of the great proprietors of estates. But something must be done to give security of tenure for the small farmer, and therefore an inducement to people to stay on the land instead of drifting more and more to cities, and already overcrowded centres of population there. This tendency to migrate from the land was checked by the Crofters' Act of 1886, and the present Bill merely extends the principle of that Act to the whole country. The Crofters' Act, so far from impoverishing the landlords, really improved their property, and made their rents more secure. The Act was denounced by Mr. Balfour just as the present Bill is 'denounced. Every one believes, however, that the former Act has proved a success, and that there can be no prosperity in agriculture until the farmer knows. that he is to enjoy the benefit of his own

improvements. I cannot profess to be an expert in the intricacies and detailed problems of the land, but I venture to say that this broad fact cannot be gainsaid,—and they go to the very root of a question scarcely less vital for those of us who live in towns, than for those who dwell in the country—and that of course because it bears so vitally and directly on the physique and well being of the whole nation. It is generally anticipated in the House of Commons that the Lords will not throw out any of our Bills on Second Reading. If this forecast should prove correct, then it will show—and let me emphasise the fact— how much has been accomplished by the Prime Minister's resolution.

THE PEERS ARE NOW I'ACED with the necessity of justifying their action, and the challenge is teaching them caution. If the House of Lords should prove to be absolutely irreconcileable, then cf course we should in the end be forced to resort to stronger measures still. But it will be much better for the Peers to accept the situation, cease to frustrate the wishes of the people ; set their own house in better order ; develop, let us hope, into what they ought to be, namely, a second cl.amber for judicial and impartial criticism and revision ; and so enjoy a long measure of popularity in a country which is fond of ancient and picturesque institutions —(provided they behave like rational beings), Now I dare say there are some of your readers who, in dealing with the House of Lords, would like to go in for very drastic measures indeed, and in fact sweep the second chamber away altogether. But I do not see they would have any chance of carrying the country with them if they attempted that policy; and perhaps they sometimes overlook the immense pressure of work which there is now on the legislature. Fre- quently it is possible to discuss in the second chamber subjects for which there is no time in the House of Commons. And then again some of the Fiscal debates which took place in the Upper House during the last Parliament were, I think, of great value and import- ance, and showed how in this and other matters the Second Chamber may play an important part in the education of public opinion. There is no objection to the Lords suggesting improvements in our Bills, and correcting any slips which may have crept in during debate in the House of Commons. All such revising powers are useful if they are exercised in a fair spirit. What we cannot countenance is a deliberate desire on the part of the Peers to wreck our legislation, not by way of improving it but by way of destroying it. Turning for a moment before I conclude, from the House to the country, may I in conclusion draw atten- tion to the extraordinary position in which the Tariff Reformers find themselves owing to the result of THE LAST THREE SUCCESSIVE BT-ELECTIONS. At Jarrow the Free Trade Vote was split up among three candidates, yet the Protectionists could not carry their man. At Colne Valley there were two Free Traders, yet here again Protection was defeated. Finally at North Staffordshire, in a straight fight, Liberalism, in the person of Mr. Stanley, did better even than at the General Election, despite the fact that the contest turned wholly on Tariff Reform, the Conservative candidate, a man of ability whom I happen to know, and who fought with energy and courage, having by no means shirked that issue, but having made it the main plank in his election platform. Mr. Harvey who addressed us not long since in War- rington, did yeoman service to the cause of Free Trade, and returned to the House of Commons scarcely less the hero of the election than Mr. Stanley himself. I expect it won't be very many months before they pay us a visit in Warrington—at least I hope so. I had an hour's talk with Mr. Harvey the other day, and he gave me a most vivid and interesting descrip- tion of the way the election was fought, and how the combined forces of Liberalism and Labour triumphed over all opposition. This is certainly the severest defeat the Protectionist Party has sustained since the General Election, and it is significant that in the House of Lords Viscount Aldwyn (known formerly as Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, Conservative Chancellor of the Exchequer) last Thursday declared once more that the hopes of Tariff Reformers are fallacious. And what of Mr. Balfour.? I had the privilege of knowing him as a golfer some years before entering the House but I have never been taken into his political confidence. Still I venture to say, and in fact am perfectly certain that MR. BALFOUR HIMSELF HAS THE GRAVEST MISGIVINGS about the policy of the yery Tariff Reformers he is supposed to lead, which makes the situation the more extraordinary. %7I am temptqd to enlarge on this, and especially on the debate we had last Monday fortnight or Monday three weeks, which was the most remarkable exposure of the weakness and hollowness of the Protectionist , case I have ever listened to. But tide and steamers wait for no one, and My boat is on the shore And my bark is on the sea, Ere I cross the main once more, Reader, here's a health to thee! A. H. CROSFIELD. Dover, August 15th, 1907.

div.head: VOICE OF LABOUR.
div.p: THE VOICE OF LABOUR.

Edited by John Workman. Readers of this column are invited to assist in making it interesting and helpful to social workers by contributing themselves. Correspondents must write on one side of the paper only, and endeavour to make their letters an notes short and to the point. A nom-de-plume may be used, but the real name of the writer should be forwarded in confidence to the Editor of the colum4, 31.5.5. must be addressed to John Workman; "Examiner " Office, Warrington and should be sent in not later than Wednesday in each week.

I am home again. Home from the sea and the ships, from the fields and the flowers. Back to Warrington. After so much sunshine and fresh air, the outlook is not inspiriting. Somehow Warrington wears a gloomy look and seems ever so dead-and-alive after a holiday. The sun is content to play on the tops of the smoke- clouds and the atmosphere is vitiated. Perhaps, if we were not hemmed in NI, ith financial difficulties ; if wh were not compelled to spend most of our time in working to make both ends meet; if it were not necessary for workers to combine in an endeavour to combat the machinations of employers ; if employers were not so harassed by unfair conditions and competition ; if we were not mentally and physically exhausted in labouring for "our daily bread,"—we might have time to make Warrington a city worthy of our dreams. The day is coming, though, when the workers will have more opportunities for physical and mental recreation. And life will be brighter and happier! if you have sunshine in your heart, Don't keep it—pass it round. To those who need it, give a part, Don't keep it—pass it round. It wasn't made alone for you, It's yours, of course, but still it's true It's meant for other people, too. Don't keep it—pass it round. You'll find you have enough to spare, Don't keep it—pass it round. 'Twill drown a lot of gloomy care, Don't keep it—pass it round. Dividing up your sunshine store Will lighten loads for those heartsore, And you'll enjoy life all the more. Don't keep it—pass it round. I have a lot of arrears to pull up. Next week, I will reply to Mr. C. E. Parker's criticism, and probably to "Rosa Canina."

pondent's figures prove that his knowledge of the political labour movement is extremely limited. It is quite true that the Independent Labour Party is an avowed Socialist organisation, and diametrically opposed to Toryism and Liberalism. How could the I.L.P. be otherwise than opposed to the parties which are fundamentally opposed to theta.? Sir Thomas Whitaker in addressing his constituents a few days ago said that he wished them to understand that the object of the Labour and Socialist parties was to build up their movements by the destruction of the Liberal party:

Tiiis is quite true. It is what we have been trying to impress upon the electors for a number of years. We are seeking the destruction of the Liberal party, and we also wish it to be understood that we aim at the destruction of the Tory party as well. I ask your correspondent in which way the " trust- worthy labour stalwarts" he mentioned have been political successes? Regarding the effective work done by Mr. Maddison, M.P., and Mr. Vivian, lt.P., where is the effectiveness of their work in the two recent bye-elections? Have not the members of the Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners publicly disassociated themselves from the effective work done by Mr. Vivian in the Jarrow bye-election where he was sent to oppose such a sterling trades unionist as Mr. Curran, M.P. ? The statement of Mr. Wilson, secretary of the Sailor's linion,—which your correspondent incorrectly quotes, —can be answered by saying that it is much easier to make an assertion than to prove it. Mr. Wilson would have a great difficulty in proving the statement he made in Warrington, at least that is the opinion of a

div.head: WARRINGTON CASE.
div.p: A WARRINGTON CASE.

Mr. Joseph Price lives just near the Market Place, Warrington, at 4k, Queen-street, and it is him we have to thank for the following state- ment : —" Four years ago I had an awful attack of lumbago," he said to one of our representatives when telling the facts of his case. " I got up one morning in terrible pain— I could scarcely get out of bed and dress myself, and the effort to get to work caused me to perspire, such agony was I in. The work I was on was not heavy, but it took me half an hour to do what I should have done in five minutes ; the torture was unbearable. The overseer asked me what was wrong with me, and when I told him he said I was not to work in that state. Then I set out for home, but how I reached there I do not know, and the perspiration fairly rolled off me. " My arms were all right, and the shoulders, too, but I bad no use in the lower part of my body, my legs being powerless. The urinary

raisecrner eyes ror a moment towards his window. He wondered if it were merely an accident, or whether she was by any faint chance thinking of him. But that little action decided him to go on with that enchanted 'bus, until she should turn it into an ordinary vehicle by leaving it. That, of course, took him to Minerva-gardens, and incidentally made him hot with resentment at the idea that she, of all other people, should be compelled to live in such a place. A mere ordinary woman might have lived there, and been well content—but not this woman. He spent the remainder of the evening outside the house in the darkness, wondering about her—wondering it he should ever by any chance come to know her or to hear her speak. For he had not heard her voice yet, even on the 'bus. She gave an exact amount in copper coin to the conductor, and the conductor understood and gave her a ticket; that was all.

That had gone on for a week. He had not dared to follow her again, but, knowing the time st which she might be expected to appear in Minerva-gardens, he had taken to haunting the spot—just for the satisfaction of seeing her come up to that grim door, insert a latchkey, and be swallowed up by the dark house. That was as rar as he had got. He puzzled his brains in vain to think how he might approach her. Desperate thoughts of setting fire to the house, or raising sal alarm of some kind, occurred to him—some iesperate deed wherein he, as the mysterious stranger, might appear upon the scene and rescue her, and so have a claim upon her for ever after. He had a mind at last to knock at the door, pretending that he had come to the wrong house, but dismissed that idea as being somewhat feeble.

As lovers will, he had got that address—No. a, Minerva-gardens—impressed indelibly upon his mind; in other words, it may be said that there was no other house in the. whole of London, or, better still, that the whole of London grew round that house, and was dependent upon it. Therefore when, in sighing over his breakfast one morning, he found that address actually staring at him from his morning paper, he started and cried out, believing for a moment that the thing could not be printed there at all, but must be some trick of his imagination. Yet there it was plainly enough: "Lost. —Purse containing five pounds in gold and a little loose silver. Also a latchkey.—A liberal reward will be given if returned to Mr. Andrew Carley, No. 2, Minerva-gardens, N." Instantly the thought occurred to Mr. Godfrey Farndale that if only he could find that purse and take it to the house to receive the grateful thanks of the owner, his way would be clear. Doubtless Andrew Carley was her father; from the appearance of the girl probably a man to whom the loss of five pounds and some loose silver, to say nothing of a latchkey, meant much. Here was a chance absolutely going begging, yet Godfrey Farndale was helpless. He thought and thought about the matter, but with no direct result.

Sitting at his window one evening he chanced to be looking out when an omnibus rumbled past, and on the top of that omnibus was the girl on her way to No. 2, Minerva-gardens. And it happened that, as on other occasions, she raised her eyes to the window where he sat. That decided it. In those eyes he read, or thought he read, abject despair at the loss of five pounds, some loose silver, and a latchkey. He pictured her going without food by reason of that loss. Scarcely knowing what he did he put on his hat, hurriedly left the house, and made his way towards Minerva-gardens. By the time he reached the house he had pretty clearly made up his mind what to do. A purse had been lost. But it was scarcely likely that the purse itself was of value; clearly the con- tents was the main thing wanted. Accordingly, when a diminutive maidservant opened the door Godfrey Farndale boldly demanded to see Mr. Andrew Carley—" with reference to the adver- tisement."

He was admitted at once, and was shown into a room on the ground floor—a dingy room, littered with books, and ledgers, and papers, in the midst of which an old man sat writing. Not an agreeable-looking old man by any means, not the sort of old man one would have expected to be related in any way to the lady with the eyea.

LALL RIGHTS RESERVED.] LOVE AND A s LATCHKEY
BY TOM GALLON,
Author of "Tatterley," "A Prince of Mischan :Nab ° "Dicky Monteith," "A Rogue in Love," "Eke Charity brho'st," "Kiddy," &c.

Unless you should chance to be a private detective, and paid by the hour for spying upon your fellow-creatures, you would scarcely care to watch one particular house for any length of time; to watch it until you seemed to know every brick of it, the curve of every water-spout and -chimney-pot, and the exact angle of every blind and window curtain; to watch it, in fact, until the policeman on his beat began to take a particular interest in you, and to mark you down for careful observation. Yet that was exactly what Mr. Godfrey Farndale had been doing for a week, in respect of No. 2, Minerva-gardens, N. Nothing very attractive about No. 2, Minerva- gardens; quite a dingy affair, as houses go. A row of iron railings a plot of ground in which some daring individual had once planted a few shrubs, which remained as a standing reproach to him ever after; and then the house, a bare, blank thing, unpainted these many years, and with dingy curtains shrouding windows that were never opened. Yet a house of houses to Godfrey Ferndale, by reason of the.fact that the jealous door shut in his divinity. It had happened in this way. Mr. Godfrey Farndale was a very idle young man, of good instincts but no purpose. Having plenty of money, and but few friends or acquaintances, he found time hang heavily upon his hands. A man cannot always be reading, nor can he spend the greater part of his day at his club; and Godfrey had been getting somewhat bored with life generally when one morning he surveyed it from the window of his chambers. (Wild horses shall not tear the address of those chambers from me, because you might then secure them and discover for yourself just such an adventure as that I am describing.) It happened that he looked out at a moment when the eyes of a girl were gazing straight into his—from the top of a 'bus; and the eyes held his for a moment gravely'and quietly before they were lowered and the 'bus was gone. Yet in that moment Godfrey Farndale had awakened, with -a start as it were, to the thought that there might be something in life after all. Quiet, nice steady eyes, with just a gleam in them that might hint at the possibility of their smiling; frank, kindly eyes, that were good to look upon because they meant comradeship; sweet eyes, with a wistful tenderness in them. Godfrey Farndale thought much about them as he went back to his breakfast.

He was at the window in good time next day, and watched 'bus after 'bus pass, until at last came that one on which she was seated. And, curiously enough, the eyes were raised once again to his window, although on this occasion they were more quickly lowered. Looking at her he noted that she was neatly but very plainly dressed, and that she had rather pretty hair under a black hat that would have looked com- monplace on another head. And, remembering the eyes, he came to a great resolution. The next morning he astounded his manservant by appearing fully dressed at an unearthly hour and demanding breakfast; further affrighted the man by seating himself at the window well behind the curtain and watching the road anxiously. When he presently started up with an exclama- tion and seized his hat and gloves and dashed downstairs, the respectable manservant decided to give notice that day—for his own safety, But Godfrey Farndale had only boarded a 'bus; had climbed to the top of it, and, with his heart going tumultuously, had seated himself within a couple of yards of the lady with the eyes. Wondering at his own daring he yet found time furtively to note that her dress, though very neat, was somewhat shabby, that she had a slight and pretty figure, and that she was quite young. When she left the 'bus at a busy point in the City, Godfrey, after a moment's hesitation, followed her, and saw her disappear within the doors of a large building let out in offices. He dared follow her no further. But he hung about all that day in the neighbourhood, and coming at night to the great doors again, was so fortunate as to see her board another 'bus for the return journey. He got on also, and secured a seat behind her. As it was a dark night and the 'bus crowded, she did not notice him. As the 'bus lumbered past his chambers he Saw. with, a sncklen.beatine of thp heart that she

"Well, have you found it, young man ?" snapped the old fellow, looking up suspiciously at Godfrey. "I have, sir," replied the young man, with a bow. "At least, to be strictly accurate," he added, "I may say that I have had the misfortune to lose it again—the purse, I mean." "I don't believe you—you've stolen it!" exclaimed Mr. Carley, rising to his feet and stretching out his hand towards the bell. "I'll send for the police; I'll have you locked up! You've run yourself into a trap--" "Stop a bit," exclaimed Godfrey, indignantly. "I was going to say that I am prepared to restore the contents of the purse, the five pounds and the loose silver; it is only the actual purse itself that I have—mislaid."

"Why didn't you say so before ? " demanded the other. "I can't afford to lose such a sum. Seven pounds, and nearly another pound in silver---" "The advertisement said five pounds,' suggested Clodfrey. "Mistake of the printer," cried old Carley; eagerly. "Don't you dare to tell me, sir, thut you've made away with a couple of pounds thut didn't belong to you ! " _ _

"Very well, call it seven, then," said Godfrey Farndale, grimly. "But what about the reward, Mr. Carley ? " "You don't look like the sort of man that wants a reward ! " sneered the other. "Well, suppose we say half-a-crown, and thank you for your trouble. It's taking half-a-crown out of what belongs to me. But I'm a generous man if a poor one. should like to ask another reward," said Godfrey, abruptly. "There is a young lady in this house, a stranger to me at present. If I might have an introduction to her—your daughter, I suppose--" "Haven't got a daughter can't afford luxuries ! " snapped Mr. Carley. "If you refer to my niece—why, you can shake hands with her if you like and I'll keep the half-crown. No fool like a young fool," he added to himself. "I have only seen the young lady at a distance," went on Godfrey, nervously. "She—she seems to work very hard, sir." "And why not ? " exclaimed the other. "Does she expect to live here in the lap of luxury and in idleness ? "

"And you will give me an introduction to her, Mr. Carley ? " suggested Godfrey. "I am a man of my word. I will give you an introduction to my niece, Miss Eva Newling, when I have from you seven pounds nineteen shillings and sixpence," replied Andrew Carley, resolutely. "The advertisement said 'a little loose silver', " urged Godfrey. "I'm an honest man, and therefore refrain from saying that it was, to all intents and purposes, eight pounds," replied Mr. Carley, with a virtuous air. "ome to think of it, the purse was worth the other sixpence." "And I am to see the lady ? "

"My dear young man, yOu may, if you like run away with her—for seven, nineteen six," brutally retorted the old man. "I don't want her. I've quite enough to do to look after myself. No sister, whether she be dead or otherwise, has a right to land her orphan daughter on a man in this fashion. It isn't fair."

"In days of old, Mr. Carley," said Godfrey Farndale, quietly, "when a man lost anything, or wanted anything, he had, I believe, one reward to offer to the man lucky enough, or gallant enough, to restore what he had lost. He offered the hand of some fair lady." "I don't read fairy stories," snarled Andrew Carley. "That's a pity, because you'd have a chance of figuring in one—probably as the wicked uncle or the overbearing father," said Godfrey. "I've a sort of suspicion that this Princess, immured in your castle in Minerva-gardens, is not too happy, and I want to try and make her happy. Come, you have offered a liberal rewhrd for the restoration of your money. The liberal reward I want is—your niece." "Settle that with the lady," retorted Andrew. "I'll take the seven, nineteen six now, if you please, and the latchkey." "I'd forgotten the latchkey," said Godfrey, somewhat at a loss. "However, that'll be all right. I must have mislaid it somewhere. Here's eight pounds, at all events. There will be sixpence change," he added, whimsically. "I have no small change; but sixpence won't break any bones," said Mr. Carley, pocketing the money. stick to my bargain. I'll send for my niece and introduce you. Come to think of it, though, I don't want any nonsense in this room, so I'll take you to her.' So it happened that Mr. Godfrey Farndale found himself, a moment or two later, bowing to his divinity, and inwardly wondering why the laws of civilisation demanded that anyone with such a crown of pretty hair should have to wear a shabby hat in the street. He was awakened from his dream by the sarcastic voice of the old man beside him, introducing him as: "My dear young friend—what is your name ? " this last, of course, in a whisper.

Then—wonder Of wonders !—he was left alone with her. He had just begun haltingly to explain what had brought him there when the head of Mr. Andrew Carley was thrust into the room again, and that gentleman barked out: "The bargain's not complete until I have the latchkey, don't forget that." Then the head disappeared again. Godfrey Farndale proceeded to explain the object of his visit to the house. He had seen the advertisement; he had been overwhelmed with grief at the thought that she must suffer because of the loss her uncle had sustained; he had restored the purse—or, rather, the contents. And he was so very glad at last to meet her. "I have seen you very often, Mr. Farndale," she said, shyly, and yet with a little twinkle in her eyes. "I know where you live." "And you've been good enough to look up at my window sometimes when you went past, he reminded her.

"Well, you see, Mr. Farndale, in all this great world of London it is nice to think some- times that one has a friend," she said, softly. "And so I got into the habit of looking up at your window, without ever dreaming that I should know you, and calling you my friend, just like a story one might make up to please oneself."

Then, of course, it became an easy matter for him to explain to her how he had thought of her in something of the same fashion; how he had dreamt about her and regarded her as his friend in all the great wilderness of London. Which was, of course, very wonderful, and wanted quite a lot of explaining. And in the midst of it she put a startling question: "Mr. Farndale, did you really find the purse ? " "I have never seen it," he admitted, sorrow- fully. "But I saw the advertisement, and I saw the chance of meeting you, and so I restored the money." "And he was willing enough to take it ! " said the girl, bitterly. "But what about the latchkey, Mr. Farndale ? "

"That's the difficulty, you see," he replied, ruefully. "I can't make my tale good, because I haven't got the latchkey. And the bargain I made with him, Miss Newling," went on Godfrey, "must be completed with the latchkey." "What bargain ? " she asked, looking at him curiously. Well, Heaven only knows how he explained the matter to her, or what tale he preached; but he must have done it rather well. For although at first she she was indignant, and stood before him in that gloriously shabby frock, furious at thus being dealt with without her knowledge, she presently began to laugh; and it was ador- able to see what a dimpling smile could come up into that tired face. And when he persisted about the latchkey she slipped out of the room, and came back holding one in her hand. . . . _ _
"It's mine," she sa-id, with a blush and a laugh. "But he won't know the difference. The servant can let me in."

"The servant shall never let you in any more, if I can help it," said Godfrey, boldly. "Just as in the fairy tales the knight came along and claimed his reward, so l'm going to claim my reward now. Oh! there's such a lot I have to say to you, Miss Newling--" "Here is the latchkey, Mr. Farndale," she reminded him, demurely. Quite a number of omnibuses pass the cham- bers wherein Mr. Godfrey Farndale once resided; but no lady with wistful eyes looks up at the windows, and no Godfrey Farndale looks down; for they have both wandered away, happily enough, into the Land of Love. And Mr. Andrew Carley, alone in his dreary old house, wonders sometimes how that young man can have made such a mistake concornina the lost nurse. con- taining a certain sum of money and a certain latchkey, because Mr. Andrew Carley found it in a drawer of his desk a week later, all intact. But, as he tells him Self, eight pounds is eight pounds, so that it is not worth worrying about.

Cyclists' Narrow Escape. • A cyclist named James Hardy, 35, Cedar-road, Altrincham, had a narrow escape of being killed on. Saturday afternoon. He was cycling along Knutsford- road, Warrington, at 3.15, when his machine skidded on the tram line opposite the Mersey Bedstead Works. The rider was thrown, and an electric car coming immediately behind carried him along a short dis- tance, untik the driver, abert Gallagher, was able to pull up. Hardy was rescued from his perilous con- dition and taken into a house close by. He was found to be suffering fr6m severe shock and slight bruises but after a rest he was able to proceed home by train. BOILING BACON, 40., 5d., 6d.per lb. ASHLEY'S.—Advt. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. Mr. G. Colley presided at the meeting of this Society on Sunday, and spoke from the text "Being almost saved." •Mr. W. Walker, of Warrington, spoke upon "The great enemy of souls," with some references to his experiences in India amongst the soldiers and natives. Many good things could be said of the natives, but their lives and characters were spoiled by the enemy of souls, their old custom of idol worship, and the traditions of their forefathers. The speaker referred to a very encouraging letter he received from the Wycliffe P.S.A. wheti in India. It was written by their Secretary (Mr. Farrar), and was full of help and inspiration to him in the hour of great need. The Secretary acknowledged the reference to his letter. Mr. F. Hickman presided at the organ.

£5OO Maintenance Arrears. The sequel to a Warrington case was heard at Lambeth on Tuesday, when Edward Arthur Ashton, ' 45, an actor, who was arrested at Mitcham on a warrant granted four years ago, was charged with neglecting to pay his wife £l5 14s. arrears due under a maintenance order granted by the Warrington justices in 1883.—The complainant said the prisoner owed her quite £5OO, accumulated arrears at 12s. per week.—Mr. Hopkins: How long has this been going on ? Witness: Seventeen years.—Mr. Hopkins (to prisoner): You are one of those* persons who manage to avoid supporting their wives.—The prisoner : I paid it on and off as long as ever I possibly could.— The magistrates made an order for the amount claimed, distress, or two months. FRESH EGGS. 16 a IS.—ASHLEY'S Sankey st.—Advt. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—IINDER THE CLOCK NOR BEST BOOTS 1N LANCASHIRE.—Advt. The Great Shrewsbury Fete. Our readers are reminded that the Shrewsbury great floral fête —which has the reputation of being the grandest flower show in Europe—will be held on Wednesday and Thursday next. Over £1,200 is offered in prizes and there will be 3,000 exhibits staged in ten marquees. Lovers of music will be afforded a rich treat, as the full bands of His Majesty's 2nd Life Guards, His Majesty's Coldstream Guards, and His Majesty's Irish Guards will play alternately and combined. There will also be a Berms of sensa- tional performances, double baloon ascents, and a horse leaping competition for £lOO in prizes. The programme will conclude with a magnificent firework display by Messrs. Pain and Sons'. Special excursion trains to Shrewsbury will be run from Warrington ' and all parts, Sad Drowning Fatality.

Mr. S. Brigho—use conducted an inquiry on Monday concerning the death of John Ball, aged 22, 15, Gaskell-street, whose body was found in the Old Quay canal at Stockton Heath on Sunday morning. The deceased's father said his son left the house at about 11 o'clock to go to work in his usual good health and he was in high spirits. There was no necessity for deceased to go along the canal to get to his work.— P.C. Dennett said that at eleven o'clock he received a telephonic message to go to the Old Quay canal at Stockton Heath. On his arrival he found deceased who had two shillings and a County Court summons in his possession. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned" there being no evidence to show how the deceased got into the water.
LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AZsTD SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Adtv. . Lymm Rushbearing Festival. _

After a lapse of over 20 years the ancient rush- bearing festival was revived at Lymm on Saturday, and attracted many visitors to the picturesque village. A beautiful pair of greys, kindly lent by. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., drew the old-time rush cart, and showed it off to great advantage. An inter- esting figure was an old Lymm resident—Henry Daniels—now in his ninetieth year, who was mounted on a grey horse which assisted in drawing the rush cart. 20 years ago. The morris dancers—all" village lads " were picturesquely attired, and went through their merry dance. The procession, headed by the Lymm Subscription Band, went round the village, and was w ell received. The festival proved very popular and promises to become a most entertaining annual demonstration. Such credit is due to Mr. James Shepherd and Mr. W. West, the hon. secretaries, for the great interest they took in the revival. Successful Local Students. We are pleased to notice among the lit Of 'successful students in the June matriculation in con- nection with London University the name of Percival Rosemarne Baxter, of ,the Warrington Pupil Teachers' centre, who passed in the second division. Mr. Baxter had previously passed with distinction when sitting for Part 11., of the preliminary examination for the pupil teacher's certificate (qualifying for admission to a training college), the subjects being English language and literature, and history.—We recently reported .that Mr. Arthur M. O'Brien, formerly of Warrington, had passed first class in ordinary grade for oils and fats at the examinations of the Glasgow and West of Scotland College in connection with the , City and Guilds of London. Mr t O'Brien has, during the past week, received official intimation that he has also been awarded the first prize of 'SI and the silver medal. This, we believe, places him first in this particular grade in Great Britain and Ireland.
