UNCLE NEP.
MY BROTHER JACK

A secret for the ears of the boys alone! Most of you, like Master Jack in the following verses, have no idea what objects of loving pride you are in the eyes of your sisters. If you have a notion about it, do not, like some fellows take their homage as your natural right, for probably you have much more reason to be proud of the loving little hearts and busy little heads that are always planning something for your benefit than they have of you. Rather let the know- ledge make you strive to be just as true and brave, and noble, and pure in reality, as they suppose you to be, so that could they see you as you are when alone, or with only the com- pany of some of your boy companions, they might still know of no cause why they should not be proud of their brothers. A ragged hat and a mended jacket, A shout, a whistle, a noisy racket,

A rough brown hand and -a heart- most tender, And wherever he is, I've a brave defender. Oh, Jack, my jewel, my own, my brother, There never, never was such another, For boys are many and brothers are plenty, But I would not give up my Jack for twenty. He does not coax me, he does not pet me, And I never kiss him, for—he won't let met- But if I'm afraid, ah, his strong arm holds me Close to his side, and he never scolds mel

What care I for the bramble hedges, The muddy roads and the tangled sedges, Or rain or snow? If we're but together, Always for me it is sunny weather! Oh, Jack, my comrade, my boy, my treasure, My partner in each grief and pleasure, There is none on earth I would place above him, But he does not dream of how much I love him!

div.head: LIBERAL CHESHIRE.
div.p: LIBERAL CHESHIRE.
DEMONSTRATION IN ALDERLEY PARK
iMr. A. J. King. M.P., and Tory Misrepresentations.

A great demonstration in connection with the Knuts- ford Division Liberal Association was beld on Saturday in Alderley Park. The weather was fine, and the beauti- ful grounds were seen at their best by a party numbering several hundreds. Mr. A. J. King, M.P., representative of the division, and Mrs. King hold a reception near the Hall. Afterwards there waslea, followed by an open- air meeting. Lord Stanley of Alderley, as president of the Association, was in the chair, and there were also present :—Mr. King, M.P., Mr. A. L. Stanley, M.P., Mr. A. A. Haworth, M.P., Colonel Brocklehurst, M.P., Mr. Theodore Crewdson, Mr. Harold Whiston (president of the Macclesfield Division Liberal Association), Mr. H. P. Greg, Mr. C. J. Holdsworth, Mr. Peter Davenport, Mr. kldarman Thompson, Mr. J. Arnold Thompson, Mr. W. H. Sherbnrn, and Mr. Joseph Smith, secretary. In a letter expressing regret that he could not attend, Mr. J. Tomkinson, M.P., wrote :—" I am sorry to miss the meeting, the more so as I should have liked to con- gratulate the electors of the Knutsford division in person on the admirable speech on the Hague Conven- tion in the House last week made by the excellent member—a speech which was the subject of universal commendation in all quarters." (Cheers.) Sir J. Emmott Barlow, M.P., and Mr. A. L. Goodson also sent letters regretting absence.

div.head: WORD FOR THE HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: A WORD FOR THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

Lord Stanley said he did not think Liberals ought to feel out of sorts because the Government they had sent to office bad not been able to do all they hoped to do. Nobody could say the Government had been lacking in effort and, in purpose. If the nation was to get through the overwhelming mass of work which Parliament undertook to transact, it must introduce some business-like methods of trans- acting it. He belonged to a House which was much abused—(laughter),—and he was not going to say a word in extenuation of any abuse they might like to direct against it, but there was one thing he would say in favour of that House. If any member of the House of Commons, or any politician coming up from the country, listened to the debates in that House, he would be struck with the great directness, promptitude, and efficiency with which the business was despatched. Some people accused the House of Lords last year of debat- ing the Education Bill at too great a length. He attended right through those debates, and his impres- sion was that they did not debate the bill at anything like the length of time occupied in the House of Commons.

The House of Lords sometimes got a little in con- fusion about matters of order because they had no person there to keep order. They were, indeed, supposed to be so orderly that order kept itself. (Laughter.) The other night they passed through the Criminal Appeal Bill. There were one or two altera- tions made which the Government did not like, but he thought anyone who attended that debate would say it was limited to people who were entitled to speak—such as eminent judges and people who knew the law,—and that the points were put promptly and seized promptly. While he did not wish to set up the House of Lords as an example as to the spirit in which it approached legislation, he did think that members of the House of Commons who wasted so much time might with advan- tage be ordered to spend some of their spare time sitting in the gallery and seeing the way in which bills were discussed and the different clauses got through. If the House of Commons could limit the right of speaking to people who had something to say the debates would be very much improved. There was not the slightest doubt a good many people spoke because they thought they owed it to their constituencies or to themselves to do so. The House of Commons 'would have to make up its mind to help the Government if they were to get through the immense mass of legisla- tion which reformers were perpetually calling for. (Hear, hear.) CONSERVATIVE MISREPRESENTATIONS.

Mr. A. J. King, M.P., who was icelcomed with cheers, spoke of the importance of keeping their Llberal organisation in an efficient condition and of not Max- ing their enthusiasm and their faith in Liberal principles. One of the things of which he thought they had the right to complain was misrepresentation by political oppon- ents. With regard to Woolwich Arsenal, statements were being made that the Liberal Government, owing to its cheeseparing policy, was discharging men wholesale from the Arsenal and causing destitution at Woolwich. He asked a question on this subject of Mr. Haldane in July, and elicited the statement that under the Conservative Government from the end of the war to the end of the late Government there were discharged from Woolwich Arsenal 4,567 men. Since the Liberals came into office there had been discharged 2,473 men. The fact was that it was a consequence of rushing into a war which disorganised industrial conditions. When we were not at war men could not be kept making things at the public expense which were not required. (Hear, hear.) Mr. King went on to discuss the question how it would be possible in the House of Commons to give a limited time to discussion without limiting freedom of speech, which was the very basis of self- government. Of course the business of the House was increasing every year, and was now enormous. Sir H. Campbell-Bannerman had tried one plan of meeting the diffiulty—setting up Grand Committees to deal with the details of bills brought before the House. Another plan he ovould support was to limit the time of individual speeches. To his mind, however, the only real solution of the difficulty was to bring in some wide measure of devolution, leaving the people of Scotland, Ireland, and Wales to deal with matters which con- cerned those countries alone. By a scheme of devolu- tion or Home Rule all round let each country deal with its own local affairs, and let the Imperial Parliament be concerned only with Imperial affairs. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion Mr. King moved—" That this meeting of the Knutsford division Liberals expresses its con- fidence in the present Goverment under the leadership of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman." The Hon. A. L. Stanley, M.P., seconded the resolu- tion. In the future we must look, he thought, for more legislation and less discuszion in the House of,Commons. Mr. Stanley demurred to the statement which had been madelthat this House of Commons was doing no work. "We have sat longer," he said," and passed more bills in the two years than any other Parliament in the history of Parliament."—(Cheers). Although he was not in agreement with the viewu of Mr. Grayson, he welcomed a certain representation of such men in Parliament for the sake of criticism.—(Hear,-hear.)

THE LESSON OF THE ELEbTIONS. Colonel Brocklehurst, M.P., speaking in support of the resolution, said it bad been said that the country were getting tired of Liberal legislation. He did not think, however, if they looked round at the bye- elections • they could see any signs of it. What they could see was that so far from being tired of ultra-Radical legislation the people seemed to think it was not going fast enough and were turning rather to ttie parties who were promising more advanced and fiery legislation than was advocated by the Liberal party. He did not think the country was at all looking to a re-actionary party like their Conservative opponents to take them back to the old days of dreamland. The country wanted more legislation, and he fancied when the next general elec- tion came round it would be found that votes would be cast either for Liberals or the more advanced wing of the Liberals, and not for the Tory candidates. (Hear` hear.)

div.head: RESOLUTION OF CONFIDENCE.
div.p: RESOLUTION OF CONFIDENCE.

Mr. A. H. Haworth, M.P., proposed a resolution which expressed high appreciation of the unselfish devotion of Mr. King to the Liberal cause, and pledged the meeting to support him when he again appealed to the constituency. The resolution was unanimously adopted. Mr. Harold Whiston (Macclesfield) moved a resolu- tion of thanks to the speakers' and to Lord Stanley for opening his beautiful park to the party. He remarked that if we had in the peerage many such men as Lord Stanley, with the same breadth of opinion and the wide outlook which grasped the fundamental necessities of social and political conditions, we should have much less talk of the abolition of the House of Lords. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Theodore 'Crewdson, in seconding the resolution, urged the members of the Association to keep firmly together. The resolution was cordially adopted and briefly acknowedged by Lord Stanley and Mr. King, M.P.

div.head: Conscientious Objector.
div.p: Conscientious Objector.

At Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Ernest Sumner, Walton-road, Stockton Heath, applied for an order exempting his child, Bessie Irene, from vaccination.—Mr. H. Greenall (magistrates' clerk) : Why? Applicant: Because my conscience forbids me baying my child vaccinated.—Mr. Greenall: You have to satisfy the Bench that/you have a conscien- tious objection.—Applicant said that as the result of being vaccinated his arm was very bad and one of his eyes had been affected as the Bench would see.—Mr. Greenall : Did the doctor tell you that? Applicant: Yes.—Mr. Greenall: You would rather your child run the risk of small-pox without being vaccinated? Applicant: I will swear my conscience says vaccina- tion will be liable to injure my child's health.—The Bench granted the application.

div.p: The Case of Ineendiarism.

At the Borough Police Court on Wednesday before the Mayor and other magistrates a little girl named Mary Potts, Turner-street, was again charged with having set fire to a portion of the factory of Messrs. Platts, fustian cutters, Lythgoes-lane on the 30th of July.—The Chief Constable said the place was securely fastened on the night in question. At 10 o'clock a person standing near the works saw the place on fire and immediately took the precautionary steps. The fire brigade came but their services were not required. Although the damage did not exceed IS, there might have been a greater amount of damage if the -fire had not been instantaniously checked, because the wood was perfectly dry. The origin of the fire was at first unknown, but it was afterwards discovered that this girl with two other girls had made it up to set something on fire. The defendant bought some paraffin oil and some matches. On the 30th of last month she bioke two windows in Messrs. Platts factory and poured the oil on to the woodwork and afterwards set fire to it. He said that the girl's mother wished the bench would send her away to some reformatory, but Mrs. Potts afterwards asked the bench to keep her child in the Union.—The Mayor said it was a very serious case. Be said, the girl had caused a great number, of people to be out of work through her bad conduct.—The bench decided to send Mary Potts ,to Darby House Reformatory School, Loan Head, Mid-Lothian, Sco)land

div.head: "THREE ORPHANS."
div.p: "THREE ORPHANS."

Two men in America were doing some work, when they caught sight of bear tracks. They followed for a while, and then set a heavy trap. Later they returned, and found that their efforts had not been in vain. There, in the trap, was a large bear, with dumb, beseeching eyes, from which the tears rolled as they might have rolled from a human being. The men shot her, and they waited until the old bear, her husband, came in sight. He was not trapped, but he was killed just as expeditiously. Afterwards three young cubs appeared on the scene, and whimpered like sorrowful babies over the killing of their parents. One of them, about the size of a small shepherd dog, climbed to the branch of the tree on which their bodies were suspended, and looked down in wonder at the still, dead faces. Another little chap sniffed feebly at the swaying body of his mother, while the third put his paws trustingly and pathetically upon the knees of one of the men whose rifles had done the work. NELLIE KEENE.

THE OWL AND THE PUSSY CAT. The Owl and the Pussy Cat went to sea In a beautiful pea-green boat, They took some honey, and plenty ol money, Wrapped up in a five-pound note. The Owl looked up to the stars above,

And sang to a small guitar, "0 lovely Pussy! 0 Pussy, my love, What a beautiful Pussy you are, You are, You are, What a beautiful Pussy you are!" Pussy said to the Owl, "You elegant fowl! How charmingly sweet you sing! 0 let us be married! Too long we have tarried: But what shall we do for a ring?" They sailed away for a year and a day, To the land where the Bong-tree grows, And there in a wood a Piggy-wig stood, With a ring at the end of his nose, His nose, His nose, With a ring at the end of his nose. "Dear Pig, are you willing to sell for one shilling Ypur ring ?" Said the Piggy, "I will." So they took it away, and were married next day By the Turkey who lives on the hill. They dined on mince, and slices of quince, Which they ate with a runcible spoon; And hand in hand, on the edge of the sand, They danced by the light of the moon, The moon, The moon, They danced by the light of the moon.

A gentleman, riding through Sydenham, saw a board with "This cottage for sail" painted on it. As he was always ready for a pleasant joke, and seeing a woman in front of the house, he stopped and asked her very politely when the cottage "would sail." "Just as soon as the man comes who can raise the wind," was the quiet reply

The squire of a certain parish, going the round of his domain, met with a poor navvy trespassing. "What are you doing here, sir ?" exclaimed the squire; "don't you know that no one is allowed to trespass here?" " Wey, Sor," replied Willy, " aw divnt knaw who's grund it is; but aw've n'yyen o' my awn, an' aw mun be on somebody else's. Aw eawnt walk anunder the grund."

div.head: IN A BIRII,
div.p: IN A BIRII,
STINCT

A traveller relates that while passing through a small forest in Brazil, he was attracted by the rapidly-uttered cries of alarm of a bird, and, wishing to learn the cause, he made his way to the tree whence he thought the sounds pro- ceeded, and, on looking up, saw that a serpent was slowly winding itself up towards a nest of unfledged little ones. While watching its move- ments, the male parent bird arrived, who, circling twice or thrice over the top of the tree, swiftly darted away further into the forest, and in a few seconds returned with a large leaf in its little mouth, which it instantly placed over the nest, and then flew up higher. Meantime the serpent wound itself slowly up the tree and reached the nest, but on putting its head over the side, started quickly back, descended the tree, and was lost in the underwood. The traveller being deeply interested in the singular incident, afterwards learnt from some of the natives that the leaf of a certain tree is a deadly poison to the serpent. But how had the bird acquired a knowledge of this? 'What mortal can say—what philosophy can explain?
"THE WAY YOU ALWAYS STOPPED."

The "Vermont Record" tells a good story of an innocent old lady, who never before had "rid on a railroad," who was passenger on one of the Vermont railroads at the time of a recent colli- sion, when a freight train ran into a passenger train, smashing one of the cars, killing sevesal passengers, and upsetting things generally. As soon as he could recover his scattered senses, the 'conductor went in search of the venerable dame, whom he found sitting solitary and alone in the car (the other passengers having sought terra firma), with a very placid expression upon her countenance, notwithstanding she had made a complete somersault over the seat in front, and her bandbox and bundle had gone unceremoniously down the passage sway. "Are you hurt?" inquired the conductol.. "Hurt I Why?" said the old lady. "We have just been run into by a freight train, two or three pas- sengers have been killed, and several others severely injured." "La me I I didn't know but that was the way you always stopped !"

div.head: LOST WILLIE.
div.p: LOST WILLIE.

A poor boy employed in Scotland to keep sheep was overtaken on the hills by a severe snowstorm. Long and bravely he kept up, and tried to drive his flock towards home by taking note of the landmarks he knew. All in vain; the snow fell fast, and before night all traces of roads and paths were lost, and poor Willie found himself alone in the hills with his sheep. As the night wore on the fatal drowsiness began to creep over him, beyond a power to resist, and without a scrap of shelter, he laid himself down among his sheep to sleep and die, for he was sure he would never wake on earth. With a smothered prayer for help, he fell asleep, and as he lay there more sheep came and huddled around him. Strange, indeed, as it may seem, the warn4th from them kept him from being frozen to death. A party from home went in search of him, and they found him surrounded by a dozen old sheep, whose instincts had saved his life. In keeping themselves warm they had kept warmth and life in him. And he lived many years to tell this anecdote of his boy- hood's peril when lost on the wild northern hillside.

div.head: WONDERFUL DOG.
div.p: THE WONDERFUL DOG.

A gentleman residing in the country had a. wonderful dog, and though he never tried to get any money by the exhibition, he was very proud of showing off the tricks to such persons as might happen to call upon him. The dog would go at his bidding into the dressing-room of his master, .and fetch therefrom any article which was named to him. "Go and fetch my left slipper!" said the master; and the dog would fetch the left slipper. "Go and fetch me a pocket handkerchief I" and the article was forthcoming. "No, not that one—a silk one with blue spots," and back went the dog to return with the proper handkerchief. This was certainly very astonishing, and all doubters were con,Tinced by the evidence of their own eyes. One day, however, the aston- ishment of everybody was considerably modi- fied by the discovery of the fact that when- ever the dog showed off there was a maid servant stationed in the dressing-room, who overheard the order, and gave the required iirticle to the animal. The owner of this marvel of canine sagacity used. to preface his direc- tions to the dog with a "poor fellow, he is getting very old and deaf," and that was the pretett for calling out the order in a very loud tone.

A Promising Pupil.—On a cold frosty morn- ing an Irish lad was late in his attendance at school, when he was severely reproved by his master. "Faith, sir," said young Pat, "it was no fault of mine at all, at all. The road was so slippery, that every step I took forward Was two backward." "Oh I you big blackguard, how can that be? If you had walked that fashion, you never could have got here by any manes." "No more I would, sir, and so I played the road a trick. I turned my back on the school, and made it believe I WBlB going home again."

"I should so like to have a coin dated the year of my birth 1" said a maiden lady of un- certain age to a male acquaintance. "Do you think you could get one for me?" "I am afraid not," he replied. "These very old coins are only to be found in valuable collections." And yet he cannot see why, when he met the lady the next day, she didn't speak to him.

div.p: THE WAY TO A MAN'S HEART.

At this time of the year the liver is very liable to get out of order; then follows lassitude, headache, shortness of temper. div.head: PHOTOGRAPHING THE EYE.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHING THE EYE.

Professor Dimmer, of Gratz, has per- fected an apparatus for photographing the interior of the human eye, which is said to give better results than any hitherto at- tained. By means of a system of lenses and mirrors a flash of light is sent into the eye, and the illuminated image of the retina is projected upon a photographic plate. The exposure is limited to a sixteenth or a twentieth of a second in order to avoid the physiological effects. The purpose of the in- vention is to obtain correct information con-
cerning diseased states of the ,retina, and the pictures are clear and full of detail.

div.head: THIN SKULLS FROM WIGS.
div.p: THIN SKULLS FROM WIGS.

The curious thinness of some skulls of Egyptian mummies of the fourth to the nine- teenth dynasties has been studied by Dr. G. Elliot Smith, Professor of Anatomy at Cairo, and he suggests that the cause may have been the wearing of heavy wigs. It occurs in both male and female skulls. It is found only in mummies of wealthy people, and the Upper classes of the period to which the phenomenon belongs are known to have fol- lowed tne fashion of wearing enormous wigs. Intermittent pressure, such as that of tL e water jars carried by modern fellaheen women, does not seem to affect the blood supply sufficiently to cause the bone to Atrophy.

div.head: HIDDEN STREAMS.
div.p: HIDDEN STREAMS.

Reference has been made frequently within the past few years to the progress of scien- tific investigation concerning subterranean streams and rivers. It is a subject of con- stantly growing importance in connection with the irrigation of desert, or partially desert, regions. , The manner in which streams which once flowed on the surface of the earth have buried themselves from sight in places where calcareous rocks abound is well illustrated by the subterranean waters of the valley of Jehoshaphat, near Jerusa- lem. As Mons. Sallior points out, the explo- ration of these hidden streams in a region covered with places sacred to three religions —Christian, Jewish, and Mohammedan—is confronted by peculiar difficulties. But enough has been discovered to make it certain that ' beneath this dry and barren-looking dis- trict flows an abundance of water, and some of the fountains famous in *Scripture story owe their existence to this subterranean source.

div.head: INSCRIPTIONS OF SINAI.
div.p: THE INSCRIPTIONS OF SINAI.

For some years past travellers in Sinai have noticed a number of curious inscrip- tions on the rocks in the wadis or valleys of the Peninsula. The earliest traveller to note and copy these graffiti was the Indian ex- plorer Foster, who passed through the coun- try on his way to the Far East in the early part of the eighteenth century. This tra- veller unhesitatingly ascribed them to the Israelites, who, according to his theory, in- scribed them during their forty years' wan- derings. Othoro, agititt, attt ibuted them to pious pilgrims to Sinai, while some were of opinion that they were the work of shep- herds. Against this last theory it was urged that few, if any, of the modern Be- douin or shepherds of the district can either read or write, how much less, therefore, those of the first and second centuries to which date the inscriptions of Sinai cer- tainly belong. All these theories have now been finally disposed of, says the Globe, by the researches of Professor Eutiny, who has mz,kie a systematic examination of the whole district in which they are found, and has carefully studied and published the texts. The real authors of these inscriptions turn out to have been Nabathwan traders, who from time to time passed through the Sinaitic Peninsula with their caravans to the markets of Egypt and Palestine, and who thus left behind them the records of their visits. The chief importance of the Sinaitic inscriptions lies in the fact that they represent the transitory stage of Nabathrean on the one hand and Neski Arabic on the other.

COLD WINDS FROM THE GLACIERS were purely local, and died away over the open sea, and Were confined to the lower strata of a few hundred metres, above which kites would not rise. In the higher strata the winds were much stronger, blow- ing at the rate of twenty or thirty metres per second at an altitude of 10,000\ metres, •as shewn by pilot balloons and telescopes. , But the winds were very irregular; the westerly component was the most powerful, and winds fron: the south were as frequent as winds from the north. It will be seen from this most important exploration of the 'higher atmosphere 'of the Arctic circle, the results of which were communicated to the rtmen Acactemy or mciences, that the winds from the south are purely local ; and that if any strag winds predominate at all, it in rather the ffesterly winds.

THE LUNCHEON.

At noon Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., entertained a large company at luncheon. Afterwards the usual loyal toasts were honoured. Mr. Allan Sykes proposed " Success to the Warring- ton and District Agricultural Society's Show" and said that all present were bound ur with the success of the undertaking. The Society had been in existence for 18 years. It had a very small beginning but it had pro- gressed until it had attained its present important position. On that occasion when they were enjoying the hospitality of Sir Gilbert Greenall, it was quite unnecessary for him to remind them how much the Society owed to its worthy president. (Applause.) He was glad to .4ay that this year the entries were up to the average. The boundaries of the Society had been extended four miles on the Cheshire side and he would like to see more interest on the part of the farmers as the show was principally for their benefit. The horticultural section, inaugurated last year under the special auspices of Lady Greenall—(applause)—was worthy of success, for it encouraged the growth of flowers by cottagers who were tenants on the estate. It was gratifying to know that the entries in that section had increased. He was sorry that the open classes for gentlemen gardeners had uot been better supported. In proposing the toast he coupled with it the name of Colonel Legh, the vice-president of the Society, who was highly respected throughout the county. (Applause.) The toast was enthusiastically received. Colonel Legh briefly responded. He thanked the assembly for the enthusiastic way in which they had received his name, but as regarded responding for the Society he must confess he was an absolute fraud— (laughter)—a stranger in those parts,and he was ashamed to say that was the first time he had attended the Show. The toast ought to be responded to by Sir Gilbert Greenall. who ran the Show, and who in point of fact was the Show. (Laughter and applause.) The Mayor proposed the health of Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall and said they deserved hearty thanks for their efforts to improve agriculture in Cheshire and other parts of the country. ,If they had a few more landlords who took the same interest in the comfort and well-being of the farmer they would have a very happy state of affairs, even in Ireland—(laughter and applause)—although they were rather difficult to satisfy in that country. In addition to his exertions on behalf of the Warrington Society, Sir Gilbert Greenall was an active supporter of the Royal Agricultural Society, which had now achieved remarkable prosperity, the profit at Derby last year being £2,000 and the profit at Lincoln this year £5,000. (Applause.) Manufacturing towns were greatly interested in the welfare of the farming community, because if the farmers were pros- perous the towns were prosperous too. (Applause.) The Mayor concluded by paying a warm tribute to the work of Lady Greenall on behalf of the Show. The toast was cordially honoured, the company sing- ins" For he's a jolly good fellow." Sir Gilbert Greenall thanked the -gathering most sincerely for the kind and enthusiastic way in which they had received the toast and the Mayor for his kind words which Lady Greenall and he (Sir Gilbert) highly appreciated. He was sorry that they again had bad weather for the Show. They always seemed to have bad weather and yet they came up smiling every I year. (Applause.) What was more important than that day's conditions was the continued wet weather throughout the country. He sincerely hoped they would have, after all, a fairly good harvest. If it had been wet for the show but took up afterwards to enable the farmers to get the crops in satisfactorily, they would not mind having had a wet day. (Applause.) He hoped he would have the pleasure of seeing his guests again next yea:. (Applause.)

div.head: FLOWER NOW.
div.p: THE FLOWER NOW.

IThe flower show and cottage garden competition inaugurated last season has made gratifying progress and both in numbers and quality there was considerable , improvement. The officials were :-President, Lady Greenall ; judges, Mr. C. Sprackling, The Gardens, Gardenhurst, Tarporley ; Mr. Herbert, The Gardens, Tilstone Lodge, Tarporley •, steward, Mr. J. G. div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
Mr. Allan Wilkie's Shakespearean Company.

The enterprise of the proprietors of the Royal Court Theatre in arranging foNthe visit of Mr. Allan Wilkie and his Shakespearean- Company deserved well of the public, and we are pleased to state that full apprecia- tion has been nightly manifested by large audiences. The production of Shakespearean plays in these days is often regarded as a hazardous venture, but Warrington has its Shakespeare-worshippers, and to the credit of the town be it said that there is a growing demand for stage representations of the works of the bard of Avon. Mr. Allan Wilkie stands in the front rank of English tragedians and though, weibelieve, he came here as a stranger, his reputation had preceded him and many were anxious to form their own estimate as to the faithfulness of his versions of leading parts which have gained him distinction else- where. When the curtain rose on "Hamlet " on Monday evening the theatre was filled in almost every part. The unfolding of the grim tragedy was followed with tense interest, and that the performance gave satisfaction was evident from the repeated calls " when the curtain fell. Mr. Wilkie's Hamlet is a fine, realistic conception. He takes the part as to the manner born. He is melancholy, but not oppressive,and there is no tendency to the monotonoul3, for he infuses a welcome vigour into his representation. The soliloquie,s were delivered naturally, bat With the requisite emphasis,and in the fiercer passages of the play he rose to fine dramatic heights. Mr. Wilkie is blessed with a deep and pleasantly flexible voice,and not a word virlit lost to the audience. Of the whole company it is possible—to speak in terms or p,oi " badly played would quickly develop boredom, but Mr. Wilkie's company rose to the full demands upon them, and the tragic note was sustained throughout, the most being made of the many dramatic situations. Miss Carrie Baillie gave a powerful and touching pourtrayal of Ophelia, and was particularly effective in the scene where this hapless maid, after Hamlet's mad rejection and her father's tragic death, loses her reason. Mr. Alexander Marsh scored a triumph as the ghost, his recital of the Circumstances of the murder being sufficiently weird for such a strange visitant, and *Wing the assembly. It is ironical that most of the -little humour •in the play is forthcoming from grave- diggers, and the way in which they-cracked jokes and made merry while following their gruesome trade quite , tickled the audience. These parts were admirably taken by Mr. George Munro (who was also a capital Polonius) and Mr. .Edwin Beverley. The duel between Hamlet and Laertes (Mr. Paul Lovett) was no half- hearted affair, but an exciting bout Which worked up enthusiasm to a great pitch. On Wednesday evening we witnessed a capital performance of "Romeo and Juliet," in which the ti e rot es were taken by Mr. G. Alexander Marsh and Miss Carrie Baillie. Mr. Marsh was exceedingly well suited in his part, and whether pouring tender love passages into the willing ear of the fair Juliet or fighting a la mort with Tybalt he was equally good. Miss Carrie Baillie again enhanced the high opinions of her acting. A special note is due to Mr. Paut Lovett, whose Mercutio was a masterpiece. 'Twas the cause of general regret when the exigencies of the play and the sword of Tybalt terminated his merry career. 2,11. Allan Wilkie had a light evening for once, the part of Friar Lawrence not being very exacting. On Tuesday, the " Merchant of Venice " was per- formed, on Thursday "The Corsican Brothers" and " The Bells," and last night" Othello." Mr. Wilkie's strong conpany has greatly distinguished itself, and won deserved popularity with the Warrington audiences who have crowded the pretty Court Theatre. To-night, "King Richard JII." will occupy the boards and a huge Saturday night crowd may be expected to witness the thrilling tragedy.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S ATTRACTION.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S ATTRACTION.

Next week Mr. Dickie Clare's company of comedians will appear in the musical absurdity "Lucky 'Liza,', described as the funniest play ever produced. The story has as its foundation a domestic servant's breach of promise action, and the many farcial situations in which the actors find themselves cause a fund of humour, healthy, rollicking fun. The piece goes with a swing from the rise of the curtain to the finish and anyone who wants a good hearty laugh, should not fail to see it.

div.head: Annual Show.
div.p: Annual Show.

The Stockton Heath Garden Society is a go-ahead organization, and to realize what agood work is being i accomplished by the members it s only necessary to view the many `beautiful gardens which add to the brightness of this pleasant village. On Saturday the sixth annual show was held in Wildersponl Park and, notwithstanding the wretched season, there was a highly creditable display. The exhibits were neatly staged in a marquee and the choice varieties of blooms presented a very pretty picture. There was a falling off in the number of entries-380 as against 585 last year —but the exhibitors numbered 98 as compared with 88. A gratifying feature was that 63 gardens, window boxes and greenhouses were entered for com- petition—an advance of 23. Some magnificent groups of plants were arranged down the centre of the tent. A particularly striking one was ;sent by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. The centre piece consisted of hand- some cocos palms, surrounded by Madonna lilies, with a border of maiden-hair fern, and the grotfp also included celcsia and adalypha plants and panicum. Mr. T. H. Lyon's (Appleton Hall) group of beautiful foliage plants and ferns was much admired. Conspicuous were the colens of ! brilliant colours, and this splendid array of plants, I which stood near the entrance of the tent, was one of the great features of the show. The first prize for circular group was won by Mr. F. Birch. rho dis- play of dracmnia godseffiana made a fine centre piece, and the other plants comprising the group were lilies, maiden-hair fern, crotonsi eulalia, with a pretty border of blue lobelia. . Mr. J. Owen was awarded the first prize for group of plants 4ft. by 3ft.' and his display was exaeedingly creditable, especially when it is borne in mind that his greenhouse is compara- tively small. Mr. P. Cliffe was second with a very nice group which, however, lacked the variety of Mr. 0 wen's. The table decorations were very beautiful. The first prize winner showed yellow and white poppies arranged in vases and mixed with gypsophila paniculta ; the second the same kind of flowers in baskets, with trailers of asparagus spengeri ; the third, carnations; and the fourth carnations and roses. Dinner table centre pieces made an attractive show. The decorations which secured first prizes were composed of grasses and coreopsis ; the second of carnations and gypsophila; the third of carnations; and the fourth of galgea and stocks. In the rose section Mr. Broady won the Silver bowl for the second time, and conse- quently it becomes his own property. He showed six distinct varieties. Sweet peas were one of the best features of the exhibition. Mr. H. Lyon ' obtained the first prize with three vases of choice varieties, arranged with gypsophila, and the second award went to Mr. J. D. Cannell, who had introduced kuaking grass among the flowers, with striking effect. The new varieties exhibited included King Edward VII. (scarlet), Gladys Unwin (pale pink), Miss Wilmot (pink), and Dorothy Eckford (white). Violas are exceedingly well grown at Stockton Heath, and Mr. W. A. Timperley, who won first prize, showed some lovely specimens. The indoor bouquets were very pretty, Miss E. Plinston winning first prize with an exceptionally handsome one composed of lilies and white roses, arranged with gypsophila. Miss E. A. Hall, the second prize winner, shnwed a fine bouquet of streptocarpus and asparagus ferns. In the class for outdoor bouquets, Mrs Norrington was first with a shower bouquet of sweet peas and roses and Mr. J. Moore was second with an effective arrangement of phlox drummondi and gypsophila. The vegetable classes suffered most through the unfavourable weather, the kidney beans and runner beans being very poor. The petatoes were excellent and the cabbages also were very well grown. The gardens inspected by the judges were splen- didly kept and showed what a great interest their owners take in the cultivation of flovters and vege- tables. The judges gave preference to the gardens in which flowers and vegetables were grown together. In the open class for the best kept and best stocked garfien Mr. J. Muskett secured the first prize with an exceedingly creditable display. The duties of judges were ably discharged by the following :—Classes for gardens, greenhouses and window-boxes, Mr. Poulton and Mr. Wilkinson; plants (including groups) and flowers, Mr. Jones and Mr. Poulton; fruit, vegetables, wild flowers, &c., Mr. Parkinson and Mr. Smith.

In addition to the groups of plants sent by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bar!., and Mr. T. H. Lyon there were several other interesting exhibits wilich were not for scompvtitiou. Aaaerman w:--Boiton, deputy mayor, sent a beautiful display of orchids, and also palms and ferns. Messrs. Robert Kerr and Son had a large show of plants; Mr. J. Mynekyne sent five pretty hanging baskets; Mr. W. Bainbridge exhibited a hydrangea with a mass of bloom; Mr. Mooro, shallots and beet- root; Mr. T. Broady, gooseberries; Mr. R. Tickle, sweet peas; and Mrs. Massey, fruit. A great attrac- tion was Mr. Ward's hive of bees, together with a show of honey slid wax.
OPENING BY LADY BROOKE. GARDENING AS A PASTIME FOR ALL.

There was a large attendance at the opening of the show by Lady Brooke, of Norton Priory. Mr. Vera B. Davies presided and amongst those present were :—Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart.,Mrs. Henry Greenall, Mrs. Lyon, Mrs. Broadbent and the Misses Broadbent, the Revs. James Collins and H. V. Pigot, Mr. C. Plinston (chair- man of the committee and hon. treasurer), Mr. W. H. Woodcock (vice-chairman), and Mr. A. Fawcett (hon. secretary). . _ _ _ _

The Chairman said it was his first duty on behalf of the Society to offer Lady Brooke a very hearty welcome ' on coming to open their show. Sir Richard and Lady Brooke had always been good friends of the Society and the members had had the opportunity of going through the grounds at Norton Priory on several occa- sions. As regarded the show, he supposed they were getting more ambitious as they grew older and that was their first attetrpt at a show in the open air. The committee thought the Church Institute was too cramped for the purpose and therefore ventured upon the change. He would like to take the opportunity of thanking the directors of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., for so kindly allowing the Society the use of those grounds. It had been suggested to him that Wilderpool was not quite the place for Stockton Heath Show, as it was part of that borough, and he ought to explain that the committee tried to get a site in Stockton Heath, but they were not successful. They had, however, strong hopes of getting a very good site in the village next year. So far as he was concerned, he had always looked upon Wilderspool as an integral part of Stockton Heath—(laughter)---and he did not think they were going out of their bounds in having the show there. He thought everyone would agree that it was a very suitable position. (Hear, hear.) As regarded the show, the visitors would judge for themselves. If it was not as good as usual, they could easily put the blame on the wretched summer they had had. His garden had suffered and no doubt other people's were the same. He was glad the Society was making progress. The Secretary told him they had 156 new members this year—and that sounded satisfactory. (Hear, hear.) They were indebted to the ladies for arranging the tea tent and to the Society's orchestra for tho interesting programme which would be submitted. The Latchford section was taking a keen interest in the work of the Society and was going forward.A ntunber of essays had been written in connectien with the objects of the Society by boys and girls in Stockton Heath schools and some of them were very interesting. Mr. Woodcock had kindly gone through thorn and acted as judge. The Society was doing its best to encourage a bye of gardening in the neighbourhood, and he thought anyone going through Stockton Heath would agree that the gardens and the appearance of the place were better than they were a year or two ago. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the improve- ment would be maintained. (Applause.) Lady Brooke, who had a cordial reception, said it was a genuine satisfaction to her to be present and to hear such gratifying accounts of the growth and pro- gress of the Stockton Heath Garden Society. The interest taken in it by those residing in the neighbour- hood ever increased, as was shown by the growth in the number of garden exhibits which were 63 this year, as against 40 last year, and also by the formation of a children's section—a development worthy of all praise. (Hear, hear.) She considered that the work of societies like theirs, amongst both young and old, wss of the greatest value, especially in these days when the tendency was for everyone to flock into the already over-crowded towns and neglect the simpler, quieter and more healthy joys and pleasures of a country life. Some, however, had no choice in the matter and were forced to live in crowded streets and for those that Society provided by the prizes offered for window boxes and window plants. If these window boxes were universal, what a transformation would be worked in our towns ! Our streets would be full of beauty and interest, instead of the dull and dingy aspect they now too often presented; and there could be no doubt that the happiness and, she believed, the health of all would be thereby increased by the brightening of their sur- roundings. The love of nature and of the cultivation of a garden,once implanted, would take such a firm root that it would never be eradicated, and nothing, she was certain, could be more worthy of effort than to supply a thoroughly healthy, interesting, and engrossing pastime in which young and old, rich and poor alike could share. Also it was a hobby in which everyone started even, for there was no pursnit in which real knowledge, care and love was more richly repaid. It was by no means the rich who invariably carried off the honours. They might go to large and pretentious gardens, and fin-4

plants dwindling away, fighting for life as it were, at best dragging on a miserable existence, while at the cottage opposite, if it be the home of a true gardener, they might see the same kind of plants growing in such luxuriance as to be almost a weed. The reason was not far to seek. It consisted simply in the love of the plant for its own sake and the consequent unremitting care. and attention bestowed upon it. The ideal garden, to her mind, was one within the reach of all or nearly all. It might be larger in some cases that in others, but it was one in which each individual plant was known and r cared for, whether it be the geranium in the cottage window,the ferns in a window box, the roses and holly- hock in cottage gardens, or the more important herbace- ous border or conservatories and forcing houses, ahere was but one element of success, and that was personal love, care and attention. Without that, nobody would be a successful gardener. It had been said that he who made a blade of grass to grow where none grew before was a benefactor to the human race. She thought that all who belonged to the Stockton Heath Garden Society could fairly claim that high praise, and she hoped most earnestly that their efforts would be crowned with every success and that the number of their members might even increase and multiply. (Applause.) Mr. C. Plinston proposed a vote of thanks to Lady Brooke for her kindness in opening the show. He said that as their show grew, they felt all the more anxious to secure ladies or gentlemen of position and eminence in the district to perform that interesting ceremony. They were greatly indebted to Mrs. Lyon, who was one of their best friends, for her good offices in persuading Lady Brooke to attend, and they were sure her lady- ship's presence would do much to help forward the work of the Society. (Applause.) Mr. W. H. Woodcock seconded and said he had no doubt Lady Brooke's kindly words of advice would stimulate the efforts of all who had the Society's work at heart.

The vote was heartily accorded. Mr. E. W. Bindloss moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Vero B. Davies for presiding and said they were also deeply indebted to him for so often throwing open his grounds to the members of the Society. It seemed a great pity that so many thousands of our people should have to live in such unpleasant and depressing surround- ings and it was the wish of members of societies like that by encouraging the cultivation of flowers and the love of trees to do something to mitigate and tone down what had often been aptly described as our " Anglo-diabolical order of architecture." Stockton Heath were leading the way and they wanted the place to be a beautiful residential suburb for high and low rich and poor. (Applause.) Mr. W. Hickman seconded, and the vote having been enthusiastically passed, the opening ceremony ended. The Society now boasts an orchestra of its own and during the afternoon the members played selections in admirable style under the conductorship of Mr. F. Pendlebury. The programme was as follows :—March, " Athalie, Mendelssohn ; overture "Marionettes," Gurlitt ; waltz " Passing Clouds," Prout ; suite, "Language of Flowers "Cowen ' • overture, "Lyre d'or," Hermann; gavotte, Sprites" Sutton: waltz, 'Merry Widows." Lehar ; dance," Henry Vlll,"German ; over- ture," Bohemian Girl," Balfe ; Suite, "Rural Scenes," Matt; gavotte," L'ingenue," Arditi ; waltz, "Bitter Sweet," Lothian ; overture, "Figaro," Mozart; dance, '"Loin cinßal," Gillett. In the evening the Walton Brass Band played for dancing, Mr. W. Gornall conducting. There were many visitors to the show during the after- noon and evening and the proceedings • were most successful, affording gratifying evidence of the progress of the Society.

of Chest Disease.

It has been for many years an established fact that CONSUMPTION. ASTHMA, BRONCHITIS, and CATARR,H, even in their most advanced stages, and in persons of all ages, can be positively and permanently cured, but where and how the cure . can be obtained thousands of sufferers still require to know. That such a cure can be obtained right here in Lancashire. will prove of vital interest to every person afflicted with either of these complaints.

It has now been proved bey6d dispute that 4* 'IIHE ONLY PERFECT AND CORRECT I TREATMENT," and certainly "THE MOST SUCCESSFUL YET DISCOVERED" is that gener- ally known as "THE HERN TREATMENT FOR CHEST DISEASES." It is astonishing, but it is nevertheless true, that the majority of cases which have been given up as quite 2‘ hopeless " and: " incurable " can be quite cured by this remarkable Treatment, in such a short time as one, two, and three months. It is an absolute fact that numbers of cases cured by this treatment • many years ago, are still living in the best of health, never having a return of the slightest symptom and proof against every change in the weather. This Treatment takes the- disease—the CAUSE of the cough, expectoration,Blood- spitting.Wheezing and Tightness at the Chest,S hortness and Difficulty in Breathing, Night-Sweats, Pains in Chest and between Shoulders—right out of the system by pleasant and natural means, at the same time build- ing up and strengthening the whole body so that the• cure remains permanent. _ _

There is no interference with occupation, where same is followed, and the Treatment is carried out easily iii the patient's own home. A typical case of Consumption being cured is that of Mr. Adams, as detailed below. This gentleman became afflicted with that disease twelve months ago, and Was under the constant care of two well-known Manchester doctors. He was informed that he must give up his employment, leave Manchester, and never return to it. This was most disheartening news, but Mr. Adams could do nothing else but follow such definite instructions. Two months ago he left to stay with relatives in Worcestershire, and it was evident to the most casual observer that his condition was very serious—his pale and emaciated face and body at once proclaimed the Consumptive, whom someone has said "always has one foot in the grave."
It will be interesting to read of his return to Man -- chester within a month after undergoing THE "HERN" TREATMENT.

The Examiner Saturday, August 17, 1907. I SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS. TO SEE THE PEARL INSIDE THE OYSTER. An interesting application of the X-rays is for the detection of the pearl inside the closed shell of the mollusc. In a paper con- tributed to the Comptes Rendus of the Bio- logical Society of Paris, R. Dubois gives an account of radiographs which he has made, shewing a pearl inside a species of pearl- bearing mussel. He notes also that a similar radiograph of a pearl inside a shell was made by Auguste Lumiere, and exhibited at the Colonial Exhibition at Marseilles in 1906. LONGITUDE BY WIRELESS. One of the scientific applications of wire- . less telegraphy, capable of considerable ex- tension, is the determination of longitudes. To know one's longitude on the earth it is necessary to compare the local time with tint of a standard meridian. Signals sent by wireless apparatus are capable of furnishing this information where no ordinary tele- graph-lines exist. A comparison of the two methods made between Potsdam and Mount Brocken shewed that the wireless method was trustworthy, although the aerial signals were more sensitive to atmospheric influ- ences than those sent by wire.

TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of this Council was held on I Tuesday night, Mr. T. E. Plumb presiding. There were I also present :—Councillor F. Stott, Messrs. J. Grealey, F. Massey, J. Haley, Moorfield, Leach, C. Plinston (secretary), and Howliston. IRONFOUNDF.RO etcrQcios. Correspendence was read from the Friendly Society ' of Ironfounders, in reference to the Society having totally withdrawn from the Council. The CHAIRMAN said he was very sorry, but, all the same, the Society should have given them a reason why they should withdraw from the Council. THE TRANSVAAL MINERS. An appeal was react on behalf of the Transvaal miners. Mr. HALEY moved a resolution that additional copies of the appeal should be printed and sent to the affiliated branches. Mr. GREALEY moved that the appeal lie on the table. Councillor STOTT said that they as a Council were not obliged to support the appeal, but if any member would like to subscribe to the appeal he could do so with the greatest of pleasure. Mr. HOWLISTON seconded Mr. Grealey's resolution and the letter was ordered to lie on the table. THE DUNDEE STRIKE. An appeal was read from the Scottish Bleifthers Union in reference in the Dundee District strike. Mr. Haley moved that additional copies be sent for and supplied to the rest of the branches affiliated with this Council. Mr. GnxitLEy said it was an action which they should support. PLINSTON said he thought it was a great injury to men who were struggling for liberty to be treated in this way. The resolution was carried. UNEMPLOYED WORKMEN'S BILL. A letter was read from the the Leicester Trades Council asking the Council to support this Bill. The Council passed a resolution in support and decided to send a copy to Mr. Crostield, M.P. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE FEDERATION OF TRADE; COUNCILS. Councillor STorr read his report of the annual meet- ing of this Federation. He said that a resolution was unanimously adopted in favour of the painting and decorating of schools to be done when work is scarce. Resolutions were also passed in favour of local option being given to hairdressers to apportion the hours when their shops should be open so long as they keep within the maximum number of hours allowed by law. A resolution was also passed in favour of old ago pensions. The Federation also passed resolutions recommmending all the Councils affiliated with the Federation to hold demonstrations in favour of old age pensions, such demonstrations to be held during the forthcoming Parliamentary recess. Councillor Slow said he was very glad to inform the Council that be had been elected president of the Federation. (Applause). FOREIGN TRADING. Mr. BEBRINGTON said he had a matter to bring before the Council and that was in reference to the Co-operative Wholesale Society coming to a local basket makers works and a4ing fcr their estimate. It was given to them and they afterwards came back again to say that their price was too high. If they would reduce it they would have the order but if not the Society would go to Jersey and get the things they required made cheaper. Mr. ElowLtsTos said it was the Co-operative Whole- sale Society's business whether they got their things from England or not and not the Councils. The Cilairtm AN also said it had nothing to do with the Council. The Co-operative Society went out of the country to get their things because they would be able to make a greater amount of dividend.

RUGBY FOOTBALL. _- MEETING OF THE N.U. GENERAL COMMITTEE. A meeting of the General Committee of the Northern Rugby Union was held in Manchester, on Tuesday even- ing, Mr. H. Ashton (Warrington) occupying the chair. Permission was granted to the following clubs to charge for admission to trial matches ; the whole of the pro- ceeds to be devoted to charities, viz., Wigan, Runcorn, Batley, Rochdale Hornets, Hunslet, Leigh, and War- rington. It was resolved that the hon. secretary of the union (Mr. Joseph Platt) be given authority to grant permission to clubs to take gate money at trial matches subject to the proceeds being wholly devoted to charity.

Dear Sir, I beg to say how wonderfully I am improving under your special Treatment for Consumption in so short a time, it beteg only TWO WEEKS since I com- menced the Treatment. History of Mr. Adams'case Began to feel ill in August last year, and in September (next month) broke a blood-vessel at the back of left lung, bringing up over a gill of blood, and immediately began to lose weight and strength. Blood- spitting continued at intervals up to the commence- , , ment of Treatment. - Prominent signs of Consumption in left lung, which soon extended to the right. Sharp pains between shoulders and in left lung. Great shortness of breath on slightest exertion, even on walking a little. Con- stant expectoration of yellow phlegm, somewhat like - cheese. ' Troublesome and constant cough. Pain over • stomach. Night-sweats. Very weak. Lost 18 pounds. Voice extremely weak and husky. Under two Man-- chester doctors, who could do nothing for him, but advise him to leave Manchester for good. Altogether a very severe case. The reader will understand the extreme anxiety Mr. Adams' condition was to himself, his wife, relatives, and friends. What must be a man's feelings, when he knows that be has practically been condemned to death, by • Consumption, and that all the usual so-called "remedies" and doctors have failed, and that he may never work again for those dependant upon him, but that be will he a constant burden and expeuse to him- - , self and others until the disease has done its work? This anxiety was largely increased, when Mr. Adams' "- last doctor, making 41. professional visit to the sufferer's- ' mother-in-faw mentioned that "there was absolutely no ' hope of his recovery, that he had gone too far." This information was naturally withheld from the sufferer at the time. Fortunately for Mr. Adams a Manchester payer was sent him containing a statement proving that Consump- tion and in fact all chest diseases could be cured by ' 'TETE " HERN " TREATMENT FOR CHEST IL DISEASES of 12, BRAZENNOSE STREE MANCHESTER. He immediately got into communica- tion with Mr. Hem himself, stated his case, and obtained an opinion, the resul tof which was that Mr. Adams, after consulting his friends, decided to place himself under this Treatment for a month.
